      "slug": "adr/pr-contribution-guidelines",
      "html": "<h1>ADR: PR Contribution Guidelines</h1>\n<ul>\n<li><strong>Status:</strong> Accepted</li>\n<li><strong>Date:</strong> 2026-04-13</li>\n<li><strong>Author:</strong> @chaodu-agent</li>\n</ul>\n<hr />\n<h2>1. Context &amp; Problem Statement</h2>\n<p>OpenAB is growing and accepting external contributions. Without a clear PR standard, we see PRs that:</p>\n<ul>\n<li>Jump straight to implementation without explaining the problem</li>\n<li>Don't research how existing projects solve the same problem</li>\n<li>Don't justify why a particular approach was chosen over alternatives</li>\n<li>Make review harder because reviewers must do the research themselves</li>\n</ul>\n<p>This front-loads research cost onto the contributor (who understands the problem best) rather than distributing it across reviewers.</p>\n<p><strong>Good example:</strong> Issue #224 / PR #225 (voice message STT) included a thorough prior art investigation — comparing OpenClaw's <code>audio-transcription-runner.ts</code> preflight pipeline with Hermes Agent's <code>transcription_tools.py</code> local-first approach, producing a clear comparison table, and explaining why OpenAB chose a simpler OpenAI-compatible endpoint design.</p>\n<h2>2. Decision</h2>\n<p>Establish a standard PR template and tiered contribution guidelines. All PRs document the problem, approach, tradeoffs, and alternatives. Architectural and runtime changes additionally require prior art research (at minimum OpenClaw and Hermes Agent). Docs-only, chore, CI, release, and trivial bug fixes use a lighter process.</p>\n<h3>Required PR Sections</h3>\n<p>Every PR must include these sections in its description:</p>\n<table>\n<thead>\n<tr>\n<th>#</th>\n<th>Section</th>\n<th>Purpose</th>\n</tr>\n</thead>\n<tbody>\n<tr>\n<td>0</td>\n<td><strong>Discord Discussion URL</strong></td>\n<td>Strongly recommended. Link to the prior Discord discussion. If none exists, explain context in the PR description.</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>1</td>\n<td><strong>What problem does this solve?</strong></td>\n<td>Pain point or requirement in plain language. Link the related issue.</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>2</td>\n<td><strong>At a Glance</strong></td>\n<td>ASCII diagram showing the high-level flow, architecture, or where the change fits in the system. &quot;N/A&quot; for docs-only or trivial changes.</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>3</td>\n<td><strong>Prior Art &amp; Industry Research</strong></td>\n<td>Required for architectural/runtime changes. &quot;Not applicable&quot; with reason for docs/chore/CI/release/trivial fixes.</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>4</td>\n<td><strong>Proposed Solution</strong></td>\n<td>Technical approach, architecture decisions, key implementation details.</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>5</td>\n<td><strong>Why This Approach</strong></td>\n<td>Why this over the alternatives from research. Tradeoffs and limitations.</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>6</td>\n<td><strong>Alternatives Considered</strong></td>\n<td>Approaches evaluated but not chosen, and why.</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>7</td>\n<td><strong>Validation</strong></td>\n<td>Relevant checks for the PR type: Rust, Helm, CI, or docs validation as applicable.</td>\n</tr>\n</tbody>\n</table>\n<h3>Tiered Prior Art Research</h3>\n<p>Prior art research is <strong>required</strong> for PRs that touch architectural, runtime, agent, scheduling, delivery, or persistence concerns. Contributors must research at minimum these two projects:</p>\n<table>\n<thead>\n<tr>\n<th>Project</th>\n<th>Why it's a reference</th>\n</tr>\n</thead>\n<tbody>\n<tr>\n<td><a href=\"https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw\">OpenClaw</a></td>\n<td>Largest open-source AI agent gateway. Plugin architecture across 7+ messaging platforms. Mature patterns for media, security, session management.</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td><a href=\"https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent\">Hermes Agent</a></td>\n<td>Nous Research's self-hosted agent. Gateway architecture across 17+ platforms. Strong prior art on messaging, tool integration, and service management.</td>\n</tr>\n</tbody>\n</table>\n<p>For each project, document:</p>\n<ul>\n<li>How they solve the same problem (with links to source code or docs)</li>\n<li>Key architectural decisions they made</li>\n<li>What we can learn from their approach</li>\n</ul>\n<p>If neither project addresses the problem, state that explicitly with evidence.</p>\n<p>For <strong>docs-only, chore, CI, release, or trivial bug fixes</strong>, write &quot;Not applicable — [reason]&quot; in the prior art section.</p>\n<h3>Research Flow</h3>\n<pre><code class=\"language-text\">Contributor researches prior art\n        │\n        ▼\n┌───────────────────────┐     ┌──────────────────────────────────┐\n│ Finds better pattern  │────►│ Adopts it (we benefit)           │\n└───────────┬───────────┘     └──────────────────────────────────┘\n            │\n            ▼\n┌───────────────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────────────────────┐\n│ Finds different pattern   │►│ Documents why we diverge         │\n└───────────┬───────────────┘ │ (reviewers understand tradeoff)  │\n            │                 └──────────────────────────────────┘\n            ▼\n┌───────────────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────────────────────┐\n│ Finds nothing relevant    │►│ States so explicitly             │\n└───────────────────────────┘ │ (saves reviewers from searching) │\n                              └──────────────────────────────────┘\n</code></pre>\n<h2>3. Implementation</h2>\n<table>\n<thead>\n<tr>\n<th>Phase</th>\n<th>Deliverable</th>\n<th>Description</th>\n</tr>\n</thead>\n<tbody>\n<tr>\n<td><strong>1</strong></td>\n<td><code>.github/pull_request_template.md</code></td>\n<td>Auto-populated PR form with all required sections</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td><strong>2</strong></td>\n<td><code>CONTRIBUTING.md</code></td>\n<td>Contributor guide explaining the tiered guidelines and linking to this ADR</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td><strong>3</strong></td>\n<td>Review process update</td>\n<td>Reviewers check for prior art section completeness</td>\n</tr>\n</tbody>\n</table>\n<h2>4. Alternatives Considered</h2>\n<h3>Option 1: No formal template — rely on reviewer feedback</h3>\n<ul>\n<li>Pros: zero contributor friction</li>\n<li>Cons: inconsistent quality, reviewers repeat the same feedback, research burden falls on reviewers</li>\n</ul>\n<h3>Option 2: Strict mandatory template everywhere</h3>\n<ul>\n<li>Pros: uniform quality across all PRs</li>\n<li>Cons: excessive overhead for trivial/docs/small fixes; may discourage contributions</li>\n</ul>\n<h3>Option 3: Tiered policy by PR type (adopted)</h3>\n<ul>\n<li>Pros: full prior-art analysis for architectural changes, lighter structure for minor PRs</li>\n<li>Cons: requires defining the boundary between &quot;minor&quot; and &quot;architectural&quot;</li>\n</ul>\n<h2>5. Open Questions</h2>\n<ol>\n<li>Should we enforce the prior art section via CI (e.g., a bot that checks for the section headers)?</li>\n<li>Should we maintain a living doc of &quot;how OpenClaw/Hermes do X&quot; to reduce per-PR research burden?</li>\n<li>Are there other mandatory reference projects beyond OpenClaw and Hermes?</li>\n</ol>\n<h2>Consequences</h2>\n<ul>\n<li><strong>Positive:</strong> Higher-quality PRs, faster reviews, architectural consistency, less reinventing the wheel</li>\n<li><strong>Negative:</strong> Higher upfront cost for contributors on architectural PRs; may slow down first-time contributions</li>\n<li><strong>Mitigation:</strong> Clear examples (PR #225), PR template auto-populates sections, tiered policy keeps docs/chore/CI contributions lightweight</li>\n</ul>\n<h2>References</h2>\n<ul>\n<li>Issue #224 / PR #225 — exemplary prior art research (STT: OpenClaw vs Hermes Agent comparison)</li>\n<li><a href=\"https://avasdream.com/blog/openclaw-channels-messaging-deep-dive\">OpenClaw Channel &amp; Messaging Deep Dive</a></li>\n<li><a href=\"https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/messaging/\">Hermes Agent Messaging Gateway</a></li>\n</ul>\n",
      "data": {
        "title": "ADR: PR Contribution Guidelines"
      }
    },
    {
      "slug": "adr/pr-review-loop",
      "html": "<h1>ADR: OpenAB PR Review Loop</h1>\n<p><strong>Status:</strong> Amended<br />\n<strong>Date:</strong> 2026-06-18<br />\n<strong>Author:</strong> chaodu-agent</p>\n<h2>Context</h2>\n<p>OpenAB's PR review workflow currently relies on manual triggers — a human @mentions the review bot in Discord to initiate a review. This works well for ad-hoc reviews but does not scale for repositories with frequent PR activity. Maintainers want automated PR reviews that:</p>\n<ol>\n<li>Trigger automatically when a PR is opened or updated</li>\n<li>Show review status as a commit status (🟡 pending → ✅/❌ complete)</li>\n<li>Preserve the full review process in a Discord thread for auditability</li>\n<li>Post a single aggregated comment on the PR (hiding previous comments)</li>\n<li>Work with the existing OpenAB agent running on ECS Fargate (long-lived)</li>\n</ol>\n<p>The agent should not need to be ephemeral — it stays running and receives review requests like any other Discord message.</p>\n<h2>Decision</h2>\n<p>Use a <strong>GitHub Action → Discord Webhook → OpenAB (ECS)</strong> architecture with GitHub Commit Status API for check status feedback.</p>\n<h3>Why Commit Status API (not Check Runs)</h3>\n<p>Check Runs API requires a GitHub App with <code>checks:write</code> permission. Commit Status API works with a standard PAT or fine-grained token (<code>commit statuses: write</code>), which the agent already has via <code>gh</code> CLI auth. This avoids creating an additional GitHub App solely for status reporting.</p>\n<h3>Why Discord Webhook</h3>\n<ul>\n<li>Simplest setup — only one secret (webhook URL), no Bot Token management</li>\n<li>Webhook messages posted to a channel will trigger OpenAB's existing message pipeline via @mention</li>\n<li>OpenAB auto-creates a thread for the conversation (existing behavior)</li>\n</ul>\n<h3>Configuration Prerequisites</h3>\n<p>Discord webhook messages are flagged <code>author.bot == true</code> at the API level. OpenAB's Discord adapter defaults to <code>allow_bot_messages: &quot;off&quot;</code>, which silently drops bot messages. For this automation to work, the deployment <strong>must</strong> configure one of:</p>\n<ol>\n<li>Set <code>allow_bot_messages: &quot;mentions&quot;</code> — allows bot messages that @mention the agent</li>\n<li>Add the webhook's author ID to <code>trusted_bot_ids</code></li>\n</ol>\n<p>These settings are configured in the OpenAB ECS task definition's environment variables or the agent's runtime configuration file.</p>\n<p><strong>Example (ECS environment variable):</strong></p>\n<pre><code>DISCORD_ALLOW_BOT_MESSAGES=mentions\n</code></pre>\n<p><strong>Example (config.toml):</strong></p>\n<pre><code class=\"language-toml\">[discord]\nallow_bot_messages = &quot;mentions&quot;\n</code></pre>\n<p>Without this, the webhook @mention will be ignored and reviews will never trigger.</p>\n<h2>Amendment: Reactive → Scheduled Polling (2026-06-18)</h2>\n<h3>Problem with Reactive Mode</h3>\n<p>The original reactive design (<code>pull_request_target</code> trigger) fires a webhook on every push. While GitHub Actions' <code>concurrency</code> group cancels in-flight runs, once a Discord webhook is delivered it cannot be recalled. This causes:</p>\n<ol>\n<li>Rapid pushes spawn multiple concurrent agent review sessions in Discord</li>\n<li>Agent callbacks race — stale reviews may overwrite fresh status</li>\n<li>Wasted compute and API tokens on superseded commits</li>\n</ol>\n<h3>Solution: Scheduled Polling</h3>\n<p>Replace the event-driven trigger with a <code>schedule</code> cron job that polls every 5 minutes:</p>\n<pre><code class=\"language-yaml\">on:\n  schedule:\n    - cron: '*/5 * * * *'\n  workflow_dispatch: {}\n</code></pre>\n<p><strong>Polling logic per open PR:</strong></p>\n<table>\n<thead>\n<tr>\n<th>HEAD commit status</th>\n<th>Action</th>\n</tr>\n</thead>\n<tbody>\n<tr>\n<td><code>pending</code> (&lt; 30 min)</td>\n<td><strong>Skip</strong> — previous review still in progress</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td><code>pending</code> (≥ 30 min)</td>\n<td><strong>Trigger</strong> — stale, agent likely missed it</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td><code>success</code></td>\n<td><strong>Skip</strong> — already reviewed this SHA (LGTM)</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td><code>failure</code></td>\n<td><strong>Skip</strong> — already reviewed this SHA (CHANGES REQUESTED); new push = new SHA = auto-triggers</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td><code>error</code> / none</td>\n<td><strong>Trigger</strong> — needs review (new SHA or webhook previously failed)</td>\n</tr>\n</tbody>\n</table>\n<p>The 30-minute stale timeout handles the case where the agent is down or missed the webhook — the status would otherwise stay <code>pending</code> indefinitely, blocking further reviews.</p>\n<p>This guarantees <strong>at most one in-flight review per PR</strong> at any time, regardless of push frequency.</p>\n<h3>Trade-offs vs Reactive Mode</h3>\n<table>\n<thead>\n<tr>\n<th>Aspect</th>\n<th>Reactive (old)</th>\n<th>Scheduled (new)</th>\n</tr>\n</thead>\n<tbody>\n<tr>\n<td>Latency</td>\n<td>Immediate on push</td>\n<td>Up to 5 min (best-effort; may lag under GH load)</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Duplicate reviews</td>\n<td>Possible (webhook already sent)</td>\n<td>Extremely unlikely (skip if pending; narrow race only)</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>GitHub Actions minutes</td>\n<td>Per-push (many short runs)</td>\n<td>Fixed (one run per 5 min)</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Complexity</td>\n<td>Simple trigger</td>\n<td>Polling + state check logic</td>\n</tr>\n</tbody>\n</table>\n<h3>Why This Is Acceptable</h3>\n<ul>\n<li>5-minute latency is fine for code review (not user-facing)</li>\n<li>Eliminates duplicate-review bugs without agent-side dedup (agent SHA validation remains as belt-and-suspenders for narrow race)</li>\n<li><code>workflow_dispatch</code> allows manual trigger for urgent reviews</li>\n<li>Reduces GitHub Actions billing (one run covers all PRs)</li>\n<li><strong>Cron caveat:</strong> GitHub Actions <code>schedule</code> is best-effort — actual interval may be 5–25 min during platform congestion. This is acceptable since review latency is not user-facing.</li>\n</ul>\n<h3>Stale Timeout Rationale (30 minutes)</h3>\n<p>The 30-min threshold is based on observed review completion times: typical reviews finish in 5–15 minutes (LLM processing + GitHub API calls). A legitimate review exceeding 30 min is rare (only very large PRs with many files). If re-triggered, the agent validates HEAD SHA and will skip if the original session is still active — so a false stale trigger is harmless.</p>\n<h3>Fork PRs &amp; <code>safe-to-review</code> in Scheduled Mode</h3>\n<p>The scheduled poller runs on <code>schedule</code> events (base repo context), so it has full access to secrets. The <code>safe-to-review</code> label bypass is preserved in the jq filter — PRs with untrusted <code>author_association</code> are included if the label is present. Fork PRs are handled the same as before: the poller can set statuses and fire webhooks for any open PR regardless of source, since it operates in the base repo context.</p>\n<h2>Architecture</h2>\n<pre><code>┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐\n│  Cron: every 5 minutes (schedule) / manual (workflow_dispatch)       │\n└───────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────┘\n                            │ polls open PRs\n                            ▼\n┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐\n│  GitHub Action (.github/workflows/pr-bot-review.yml)                │\n│                                                                     │\n│  For each eligible PR:                                              │\n│  1. Check HEAD commit status for &quot;OpenAB PR Review&quot;                 │\n│     - pending (&lt; 30 min) → SKIP (review still in progress)         │\n│     - pending (≥ 30 min) → TRIGGER (stale)                         │\n│     - success / failure → SKIP (already reviewed this SHA)          │\n│     - error / none → TRIGGER                                        │\n│                                                                     │\n│  2. POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/statuses/{sha}                       │\n│     state: &quot;pending&quot;, context: &quot;OpenAB PR Review&quot;                   │\n│                                                                     │\n│  3. Discord Webhook: &quot;@bot review &lt;PR_URL&gt;&quot;                         │\n└───────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────┘\n                            │ Discord message\n                            ▼\n┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐\n│  OpenAB Agent (ECS Fargate, long-lived)                             │\n│                                                                     │\n│  Receives @mention → opens agent session (auto-creates thread)      │\n│  → Delegates to reviewer team (angle-based review)                  │\n│  → Collects findings in Discord thread                              │\n│  → Aggregates into single review comment                            │\n└───────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────┘\n                            │ review complete\n                            ▼\n┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐\n│  Post Results to GitHub                                             │\n│                                                                     │\n│  1. Minimize all previous chaodu-agent comments (GraphQL)           │\n│  2. Post aggregated review comment (gh pr comment)                  │\n│  3. Update commit status:                                           │\n│     → &quot;success&quot; if LGTM ✅                                          │\n│     → &quot;failure&quot; if CHANGES REQUESTED ⚠️                             │\n└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘\n</code></pre>\n<h2>Review Loop (Auto-Fix Cycle)</h2>\n<p>The architecture supports a closed-loop review cycle:</p>\n<pre><code>                    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐\n                    │                                         │\n                    ▼                                         │\n┌──────────┐    ┌─────────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐      │\n│  PR push │───▶│  GitHub Action   │───▶│  OpenAB      │      │\n│          │    │  (set pending)   │    │  Review      │      │\n└──────────┘    └─────────────────┘     └──────┬───────┘      │\n                                              │               │\n                                    ┌─────────┴─────────┐     │\n                                    │                   │     │\n                                    ▼                   ▼     │\n                             ┌────────────┐    ┌────────────┐ │\n                             │  LGTM ✅   │    │ CHANGES    │ │\n                             │            │    │ REQUESTED  │ │\n                             └─────┬──────┘    └─────┬──────┘ │\n                                   │                 │        │\n                                   ▼                 ▼        │\n                             ┌────────────┐    ┌────────────┐ │\n                             │  status:   │    │ Auto-fix   │ │\n                             │  success   │    │ commit +   │─┘\n                             │  (done)    │    │ push       │\n                             └────────────┘    └────────────┘\n                                              (re-triggers Action)\n</code></pre>\n<p>By default, the agent <strong>only reviews and reports findings</strong> — it does not push fixes automatically. The auto-fix loop is only activated when a human (maintainer) explicitly requests it (e.g. &quot;fix and push&quot; or option 4️⃣ in the post-review menu).</p>\n<p>When explicitly requested:</p>\n<ol>\n<li>Agent fixes the code directly on the PR branch</li>\n<li>Commits and pushes the fix</li>\n<li>The new SHA has no status → next poll cycle triggers a new review</li>\n<li>Repeat until LGTM or max iterations reached</li>\n</ol>\n<h3>Safeguards</h3>\n<ul>\n<li><strong>Max iterations</strong> — agent enforces a soft cap (3 cycles per auto-fix request) to prevent runaway fixes within a single session. The workflow's circuit breaker (30 cycles) is a hard cap across the entire PR lifetime, catching edge cases where the agent cap is bypassed (e.g. multiple maintainer requests).</li>\n<li><strong>Human-only issues</strong> — if findings require design decisions or are ambiguous, the agent requests human input instead of auto-fixing</li>\n<li><strong>Commit attribution</strong> — auto-fix commits are authored by <code>chaodu-agent</code> with a clear prefix (e.g. <code>fix(review):</code>) so the loop is auditable</li>\n</ul>\n<h3>When Auto-Fix Is Skipped</h3>\n<ul>\n<li>Any 🔴 Critical finding (correctness, security) — requires human judgment</li>\n<li>Ambiguous 🟡 findings where multiple valid solutions exist</li>\n<li>Maintainer explicitly opts out of auto-fix for the PR</li>\n</ul>\n<h2>Dedup &amp; Performance</h2>\n<p>The scheduled polling model inherently deduplicates reviews:</p>\n<h3>Primary Dedup: Status-Based Gating</h3>\n<p>The poller checks HEAD commit status before triggering. If status is <code>pending</code>, the PR is skipped — guaranteeing at most one in-flight review per PR at any time. Rapid pushes between polls simply update HEAD; only the latest SHA is reviewed on next poll.</p>\n<h3>Agent-Side SHA Validation (Belt-and-Suspenders)</h3>\n<p>Even with polling, a narrow race is possible (push arrives between status check and webhook delivery). The agent still validates:</p>\n<ol>\n<li>Agent extracts <code>__commit: &lt;SHA&gt;__</code> from the trigger message</li>\n<li>Agent queries current PR HEAD: <code>gh pr view &lt;N&gt; --json headRefOid --jq .headRefOid</code></li>\n<li>If request SHA ≠ HEAD → skip review, respond &quot;Superseded by newer commit&quot;</li>\n<li>If request SHA = HEAD → proceed with normal review</li>\n</ol>\n<p>This prevents wasting API tokens and reviewer compute on commits that are no longer relevant.</p>\n<h3>Cost Impact</h3>\n<p>Without dedup, N rapid pushes could trigger N full reviews (~5 LLM calls each for angle-based delegation). With both layers active, at most 1 review runs per push burst.</p>\n<h2>Implementation Plan</h2>\n<h3>Phase 1: GitHub Action Workflow</h3>\n<blockquote>\n<p><strong>Canonical source:</strong> <a href=\"https://github.com/linyiru/openab/blob/6ad4ef419dd131e3f718dfd9b224f3967387da94/.github/workflows/pr-bot-review.yml\"><code>.github/workflows/pr-bot-review.yml</code></a></p>\n<p>Refer to the workflow file for the current implementation. Key design points:</p>\n</blockquote>\n<ul>\n<li><strong>Trigger:</strong> <code>schedule</code> (cron <code>*/5 * * * *</code>) + <code>workflow_dispatch</code> for manual runs</li>\n<li><strong>Polling logic:</strong> iterates all open PRs, checks HEAD commit status, skips if <code>pending</code> (fresh), <code>success</code>, or <code>failure</code></li>\n<li><strong>Guard condition:</strong> skips drafts, untrusted authors, and PRs with <code>review-limit-reached</code> label</li>\n<li><strong>Steps:</strong> poll open PRs → for each eligible PR: circuit breaker check → set pending status → trigger Discord webhook → error fallback on failure</li>\n</ul>\n<h3>Phase 2: Agent Callback (Status Update)</h3>\n<p>After the agent posts the final PR comment, update the commit status (using the comment's <code>html_url</code> from the API response as <code>target_url</code> so &quot;Details&quot; links directly to the review):</p>\n<pre><code class=\"language-bash\"># LGTM\ngh api repos/OWNER/REPO/statuses/SHA \\\n  -f state=&quot;success&quot; \\\n  -f context=&quot;OpenAB PR Review&quot; \\\n  -f description=&quot;LGTM ✅&quot; \\\n  -f target_url=&quot;&lt;comment_html_url&gt;&quot;\n\n# Changes Requested\ngh api repos/OWNER/REPO/statuses/SHA \\\n  -f state=&quot;failure&quot; \\\n  -f context=&quot;OpenAB PR Review&quot; \\\n  -f description=&quot;Changes Requested ⚠️&quot; \\\n  -f target_url=&quot;&lt;comment_html_url&gt;&quot;\n</code></pre>\n<h3>Phase 3: Branch Protection</h3>\n<p>Add <code>OpenAB PR Review</code> as a required status check in branch protection rules. This enforces that PRs cannot merge until the review completes successfully.</p>\n<p><strong>Setup:</strong> Repository Settings → Branches → Branch protection rules → Edit <code>main</code> → Require status checks to pass before merging → Add <code>OpenAB PR Review</code> to the required checks list.</p>\n<h2>Token &amp; Permissions</h2>\n<table>\n<thead>\n<tr>\n<th>Secret</th>\n<th>Purpose</th>\n<th>Minimum Permission</th>\n</tr>\n</thead>\n<tbody>\n<tr>\n<td><code>GITHUB_TOKEN</code> (Actions)</td>\n<td>Set pending status + circuit breaker label</td>\n<td><code>statuses: write</code> + <code>issues: write</code></td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td><code>OAB_REVIEW_ACTION_WEBHOOK</code></td>\n<td>Post review request to Discord channel</td>\n<td>Webhook URL (channel-scoped)</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Agent's <code>gh</code> auth (PAT)</td>\n<td>Post comment + update status + push auto-fix</td>\n<td><code>repo</code> (classic) or <code>contents: write</code> + <code>pull_requests: write</code> + <code>commit statuses: write</code> (fine-grained)</td>\n</tr>\n</tbody>\n</table>\n<h3>GitHub Actions Secrets Setup</h3>\n<table>\n<thead>\n<tr>\n<th>Secret Name</th>\n<th>Value</th>\n</tr>\n</thead>\n<tbody>\n<tr>\n<td><code>OAB_REVIEW_ACTION_WEBHOOK</code></td>\n<td>Discord channel webhook URL (Settings → Integrations → Webhooks)</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td><code>OAB_REVIEW_ACTION_BOT_UID</code></td>\n<td>Discord user ID of the bot to @mention (e.g. the review agent's UID)</td>\n</tr>\n</tbody>\n</table>\n<p><code>GITHUB_TOKEN</code> is automatically provided by Actions — no manual setup needed.</p>\n<h2>Consequences</h2>\n<p><strong>Positive:</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li>Fully automated — no manual @mention needed for PR reviews</li>\n<li>PR Checks tab shows live review status (🟡 → ✅/❌)</li>\n<li>Can enforce review via branch protection rules</li>\n<li>Discord thread preserves full review audit trail (OpenAB auto-creates threads)</li>\n<li>No architectural changes to OpenAB — agent receives messages normally</li>\n<li>Fire-and-forget Action — no runner time wasted waiting for review</li>\n<li>Minimal secrets — only one webhook URL needed in GitHub Secrets</li>\n</ul>\n<p><strong>Negative:</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li>Up to 5-min latency before review starts (GitHub cron is best-effort, may lag further under load)</li>\n<li>If OpenAB agent is down, status stays &quot;pending&quot; until stale timeout re-triggers (30 min)</li>\n<li>Webhook messages lack user identity — OpenAB must allow webhook-originated messages</li>\n<li>Fork PRs: <code>OAB_REVIEW_ACTION_WEBHOOK</code> and <code>OAB_REVIEW_ACTION_BOT_UID</code> secrets are not available to workflows triggered by fork PRs (GitHub security policy). The webhook step will fail, and since fork PRs receive a read-only <code>GITHUB_TOKEN</code>, the error fallback <strong>cannot</strong> write commit statuses either — the workflow will fail silently with no status update. Fork PRs can still be reviewed manually via Discord @mention. Note: the <code>safe-to-review</code> label does <strong>not</strong> grant secrets access to fork PRs — it only bypasses the <code>author_association</code> gate for same-repo PRs.</li>\n</ul>\n<p><strong>Mitigations:</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li>Filter: skip draft PRs and untrusted authors — only <code>OWNER</code>, <code>MEMBER</code>, <code>COLLABORATOR</code>, and <code>CONTRIBUTOR</code> (returning contributor with merged PR) trigger automatic review. First-time contributors and unknown authors are skipped; maintainers can add <code>safe-to-review</code> label or manually @mention the agent.</li>\n<li>Dedup: status-based gating — <code>pending</code> (fresh) and <code>failure</code>/<code>success</code> skip review. Only new SHAs with no status or stale <code>pending</code> (&gt;30 min) trigger.</li>\n<li>Concurrency: workflow-level <code>concurrency</code> group prevents overlapping cron runs from racing.</li>\n<li>Error fallback: webhook failure marks status as &quot;error&quot;, which will be retried on next poll cycle.</li>\n<li>Timeout: stale <code>pending</code> &gt;30 min is treated as agent-down and re-triggered automatically.</li>\n</ul>\n<h2>Safeguards</h2>\n<h3>Trusted Contributor Filter</h3>\n<p>The workflow uses GitHub's <code>author_association</code> field to gate automatic reviews. Only PRs from trusted authors trigger the review pipeline:</p>\n<table>\n<thead>\n<tr>\n<th><code>author_association</code></th>\n<th>Auto-review?</th>\n<th>Meaning</th>\n</tr>\n</thead>\n<tbody>\n<tr>\n<td><code>OWNER</code></td>\n<td>✅</td>\n<td>Repository owner</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td><code>MEMBER</code></td>\n<td>✅</td>\n<td>Organization member</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td><code>COLLABORATOR</code></td>\n<td>✅</td>\n<td>Explicitly granted write access</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td><code>CONTRIBUTOR</code></td>\n<td>✅</td>\n<td>Has previously merged a PR</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td><code>FIRST_TIME_CONTRIBUTOR</code></td>\n<td>❌</td>\n<td>First PR to this repo</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td><code>NONE</code></td>\n<td>❌</td>\n<td>No prior relationship</td>\n</tr>\n</tbody>\n</table>\n<p><strong>Why:</strong> Prevents token waste and prompt-injection risk from untrusted PR diffs being fed into agent context. Maintainers can still manually @mention the agent to review skipped PRs after visual inspection.</p>\n<h3>Label Override: <code>safe-to-review</code></h3>\n<p>Maintainers can add the <code>safe-to-review</code> label to any PR to bypass the <code>author_association</code> check. This triggers the workflow via the <code>labeled</code> event, allowing untrusted contributors' PRs to be reviewed automatically after a maintainer has visually confirmed the PR is safe.</p>\n<p><strong>Important:</strong> This label only enables automatic review for <strong>same-repo PRs</strong>. Fork PRs lack access to repository secrets regardless of labels — adding <code>safe-to-review</code> to a fork PR will not trigger automation. Fork PRs must be reviewed manually via Discord @mention.</p>\n<p><strong>Note:</strong> The <code>labeled</code> event is filtered — only <code>safe-to-review</code> and <code>auto-fix</code> labels trigger the workflow. Other labels (e.g. <code>documentation</code>, <code>bug</code>) are ignored to avoid unnecessary review runs.</p>\n<h3>Auto-Fix Mode: <code>auto-fix</code></h3>\n<p>When the <code>auto-fix</code> label is present, the webhook payload includes <code>__mode: auto-fix__</code>. The agent enters an iterative loop:</p>\n<ol>\n<li>Review PR → identify actionable findings (🔴/🟡)</li>\n<li>Fix all findings → push commit</li>\n<li>Re-review until LGTM or max iterations reached (agent-side cap, recommended: 3)</li>\n</ol>\n<p>When the auto-fix loop completes (LGTM or cap reached), the agent removes the <code>auto-fix</code> label to prevent subsequent pushes from re-entering the fix loop.</p>\n<p><strong>Constraints:</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li>Only effective on same-repo branches (agent needs push access)</li>\n<li>Fork PRs: automation does not trigger (no secrets available); review manually via Discord @mention</li>\n<li>Agent must implement iteration cap to prevent infinite push→review loops</li>\n</ul>\n<h3>Circuit Breaker (workflow hard cap: 30)</h3>\n<p>The workflow enforces a hard cap of 30 review cycles per PR (across all triggers over the PR's lifetime). This is distinct from the agent-side soft cap of 3 cycles per auto-fix session — the workflow cap catches edge cases where multiple auto-fix requests accumulate. On each run, it counts how many <code>pending</code> statuses with context <code>&quot;OpenAB PR Review&quot;</code> exist across all commits in the PR. If the count reaches 30:</p>\n<ol>\n<li>Adds <code>review-limit-reached</code> label to the PR</li>\n<li>Sets commit status to <code>error</code> with description &quot;Circuit breaker: exceeded 30 review cycles&quot;</li>\n<li>Fails the workflow step</li>\n</ol>\n<p>The <code>review-limit-reached</code> label is checked in the job <code>if</code> condition — once applied, no further review runs will trigger. A maintainer can remove the label to reset the circuit breaker if needed.</p>\n<h2>References</h2>\n<ul>\n<li><a href=\"https://docs.github.com/en/rest/commits/statuses\">GitHub Commit Status API</a></li>\n<li><a href=\"https://discord.com/developers/docs/resources/webhook#execute-webhook\">Discord Webhooks</a></li>\n<li>OpenAB PR Review Spec — internal agent document (not in this repository)</li>\n</ul>\n",
      "data": {
        "title": "ADR: OpenAB PR Review Loop"
      }
    },
    {
      "slug": "adr/secrets-management",
      "html": "<h1>ADR: Secrets Management</h1>\n<ul>\n<li><strong>Status:</strong> Proposed</li>\n<li><strong>Date:</strong> 2026-06-08</li>\n<li><strong>Author:</strong> @chaodu-agent</li>\n</ul>\n<hr />\n<h2>1. Problem Statement</h2>\n<p>OpenAB's <code>config.toml</code> and agent environment frequently contain credentials (API keys, bot tokens, OAuth secrets). Today these are either:</p>\n<ol>\n<li>Hardcoded in <code>config.toml</code> (insecure, leaks into git history)</li>\n<li>Injected via environment variables (visible in process listings, container inspect, logs)</li>\n</ol>\n<p>Both approaches lack centralized rotation, encryption at rest, and audit trails.</p>\n<p><strong>Goal:</strong> Allow operators to store secrets in an external secrets manager and reference them in <code>config.toml</code>. OpenAB resolves references at boot time, holds values in memory only, and never writes them to disk.</p>\n<p><strong>Benefits:</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li>Environment variables contain zero credentials</li>\n<li>Secrets exist only in OAB process memory at runtime</li>\n<li>No secrets written to local disk</li>\n<li>External lifecycle management (rotation, encryption, access control, audit)</li>\n</ul>\n<hr />\n<h2>2. Approaches Considered</h2>\n<h3>A. Environment Variables Only (Status Quo)</h3>\n<pre><code class=\"language-toml\">[discord]\nbot_token = &quot;${DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN}&quot;\n</code></pre>\n<p><strong>Pros:</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li>Simple, well-understood</li>\n<li>Works everywhere</li>\n</ul>\n<p><strong>Cons:</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li>Visible in <code>/proc/&lt;pid&gt;/environ</code>, <code>docker inspect</code>, CI logs</li>\n<li>No rotation without pod restart</li>\n<li>No audit trail</li>\n<li>No encryption at rest (depends on orchestrator)</li>\n</ul>\n<h3>B. Native SDK Integration (AWS Secrets Manager)</h3>\n<p>Build the AWS SDK into the openab binary and resolve secret references directly:</p>\n<pre><code class=\"language-toml\">[secrets.refs]\ndiscord_token = &quot;aws-sm://openab/prod#discord_bot_token&quot;\n</code></pre>\n<p><strong>Pros:</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li>Zero external dependencies at runtime</li>\n<li>Fast, reliable (direct API call)</li>\n<li>IAM-based auth (no extra credentials needed on AWS)</li>\n</ul>\n<p><strong>Cons:</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li>Increases binary size (~3–5 MB for AWS SDK)</li>\n<li>AWS-specific (vendor lock-in if it's the only option)</li>\n</ul>\n<h3>C. Exec Provider (External Script)</h3>\n<p>Delegate secret fetching to an external script/binary:</p>\n<pre><code class=\"language-toml\">[secrets.refs]\nvault_token = &quot;exec://scripts/get-secret.sh vault/openab token&quot;\n</code></pre>\n<p><strong>Pros:</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li>Zero SDK dependencies — binary size unchanged</li>\n<li>Supports any provider (Vault, GCP, Azure, 1Password, sops, etc.)</li>\n<li>Users bring their own tooling</li>\n</ul>\n<p><strong>Cons:</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li>Requires external binary/script to be present at boot time</li>\n<li>Depends on <code>[hooks.pre_boot]</code> to provision scripts (ordering constraint)</li>\n<li>Slightly slower (process spawn + CLI overhead)</li>\n<li>Harder to validate errors (script output parsing)</li>\n</ul>\n<h3>D. Feature-Gated Multi-Provider SDKs</h3>\n<p>Build each provider as a Cargo feature flag:</p>\n<pre><code class=\"language-toml\">[features]\ndefault = [&quot;secrets-aws&quot;]\nsecrets-vault = [&quot;vaultrs&quot;]\nsecrets-gcp = [&quot;google-cloud-secretmanager&quot;]\n</code></pre>\n<p><strong>Pros:</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li>Users opt-in to only what they need</li>\n<li>Official image stays lean (AWS only)</li>\n</ul>\n<p><strong>Cons:</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li>Users wanting Vault/GCP must build custom images</li>\n<li>More CI matrix complexity</li>\n</ul>\n<hr />\n<h2>3. Decision</h2>\n<p><strong>Combine approaches B + C:</strong></p>\n<table>\n<thead>\n<tr>\n<th>Provider</th>\n<th>Mechanism</th>\n<th>Included in default build</th>\n</tr>\n</thead>\n<tbody>\n<tr>\n<td>AWS Secrets Manager</td>\n<td>Native SDK</td>\n<td>✅ Yes (default feature)</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Exec (any provider)</td>\n<td>External script</td>\n<td>✅ Yes (no dependency)</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>HashiCorp Vault</td>\n<td>Cargo feature flag</td>\n<td>❌ Opt-in</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>GCP Secret Manager</td>\n<td>Cargo feature flag</td>\n<td>❌ Opt-in</td>\n</tr>\n</tbody>\n</table>\n<p><strong>Rationale:</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li>AWS Secrets Manager covers the majority of OAB deployments (EKS, ECS, EC2)</li>\n<li><code>exec://</code> provides a universal escape hatch for any other provider with zero binary cost</li>\n<li>Runtime memory impact of unused SDK code is negligible (no allocations until called)</li>\n<li>Optional feature flags allow power users to add native Vault/GCP support in custom images</li>\n</ul>\n<hr />\n<h2>4. Specification</h2>\n<h3>Config Syntax</h3>\n<p>Secret references use URI-style strings under <code>[secrets.refs]</code> in <code>config.toml</code>:</p>\n<pre><code class=\"language-toml\">[secrets.refs]\n# AWS Secrets Manager: aws-sm://&lt;secret-name&gt;#&lt;json-key&gt;\ndiscord_token = &quot;aws-sm://openab/prod#discord_bot_token&quot;\nopenai_key    = &quot;aws-sm://openab/prod#openai_api_key&quot;\n\n# Exec provider: exec://&lt;script-path&gt; &lt;key&gt; &lt;attribute&gt;\nvault_token   = &quot;exec:///home/agent/.local/bin/get-secret.sh vault/openab token&quot;\ncustom_key    = &quot;exec:///home/agent/.local/bin/get-secret.sh myservice api_key&quot;\n</code></pre>\n<h3>Reference Format</h3>\n<p><strong>AWS Secrets Manager:</strong></p>\n<pre><code>aws-sm://&lt;secret-id&gt;#&lt;json-key&gt;\n</code></pre>\n<ul>\n<li><code>&lt;secret-id&gt;</code> — ARN or friendly name of the secret</li>\n<li><code>&lt;json-key&gt;</code> — key within the JSON value stored in the secret</li>\n</ul>\n<p><strong>Exec provider:</strong></p>\n<pre><code>exec://&lt;script-path&gt; &lt;key&gt; &lt;attribute&gt;\n</code></pre>\n<ul>\n<li><code>&lt;script-path&gt;</code> — absolute path to executable (must not contain spaces)</li>\n<li><code>&lt;key&gt;</code> — first argument: which secret to fetch</li>\n<li><code>&lt;attribute&gt;</code> — second argument: which field/attribute within that secret</li>\n<li>Script must output the secret value to stdout (single line, no trailing newline)</li>\n<li>Non-zero exit code = failure</li>\n</ul>\n<h3>Resolution Lifecycle</h3>\n<pre><code>┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐\n│ openab boot sequence                                │\n│                                                     │\n│  1. Parse config.toml                               │\n│  2. Execute [hooks.pre_boot]     ← scripts land here│\n│  3. Resolve [secrets.refs] references ← THIS FEATURE  │\n│  4. Spawn agent sessions                            │\n└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘\n</code></pre>\n<p><strong>Critical ordering:</strong> Secrets resolution runs AFTER <code>pre_boot</code> hooks. This ensures <code>exec://</code> scripts provisioned by hooks are available.</p>\n<h3>Resolution Semantics</h3>\n<ol>\n<li>openab reads <code>[secrets.refs]</code> table entries (each value is a URI: <code>aws-sm://</code> or <code>exec://</code>)</li>\n<li>For each reference, calls the appropriate provider</li>\n<li>Resolved values are stored in an in-memory <code>HashMap&lt;String, String&gt;</code></li>\n<li><code>${secrets.&lt;key&gt;}</code> placeholders elsewhere in config are replaced with resolved values (TOML-escaped)</li>\n<li>Config is re-parsed with substituted values</li>\n<li>On resolution failure: log error and exit non-zero (fail-closed)</li>\n</ol>\n<h3>AWS Secrets Manager Provider</h3>\n<ul>\n<li>Uses the default AWS credential chain (env vars → IMDS → EKS IRSA → ECS task role)</li>\n<li>Region from <code>AWS_REGION</code> / <code>AWS_DEFAULT_REGION</code> or instance metadata</li>\n<li>Optional config:</li>\n</ul>\n<pre><code class=\"language-toml\">[secrets.aws]\nregion = &quot;us-west-2&quot;          # override region\nendpoint_url = &quot;http://...&quot;   # LocalStack / VPC endpoint\n</code></pre>\n<h3>Exec Provider</h3>\n<ul>\n<li>Script must exist and be executable at resolution time</li>\n<li>Timeout: 10 seconds per invocation (configurable)</li>\n<li>Environment: inherits the same sanitized env as <code>[hooks.pre_boot]</code></li>\n<li>stderr is captured and logged on failure</li>\n<li>Script is invoked once per secret reference (no batching)</li>\n</ul>\n<pre><code class=\"language-toml\">[secrets.exec]\ntimeout_seconds = 10   # per-invocation timeout (default: 10)\n</code></pre>\n<h3>Error Handling</h3>\n<table>\n<thead>\n<tr>\n<th>Scenario</th>\n<th>Behavior</th>\n</tr>\n</thead>\n<tbody>\n<tr>\n<td>AWS API error (AccessDenied, not found)</td>\n<td>Log error, exit 1</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Exec script not found</td>\n<td>Log error with hint about pre_boot hooks, exit 1</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Exec script timeout</td>\n<td>Kill process, log error, exit 1</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Exec script non-zero exit</td>\n<td>Log stderr, exit 1</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>JSON key not found in AWS secret</td>\n<td>Log error, exit 1</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Network timeout (AWS)</td>\n<td>Retry 2x with backoff, then exit 1</td>\n</tr>\n</tbody>\n</table>\n<p>All failures are <strong>fail-closed</strong> — openab will not start with unresolved secrets.</p>\n<h3>Security Considerations</h3>\n<ul>\n<li>Resolved secrets are never logged (even at debug level)</li>\n<li>Secrets are never written to disk</li>\n<li>Secrets are not exposed to <code>[hooks.pre_boot]</code> scripts (resolved after hooks)</li>\n<li><code>exec://</code> scripts run with the same UID as openab (not root)</li>\n<li>AWS SDK uses IAM — no additional credentials needed in config</li>\n</ul>\n<hr />\n<h2>5. Helm Chart Integration</h2>\n<pre><code class=\"language-yaml\"># values.yaml\nsecrets:\n  enabled: true\n  aws:\n    region: &quot;&quot;              # defaults to pod's region\n    endpointUrl: &quot;&quot;         # optional VPC endpoint\n  exec:\n    timeoutSeconds: 10\n  refs:\n    discord_token: &quot;aws-sm://openab/prod#discord_bot_token&quot;\n    openai_key: &quot;aws-sm://openab/prod#openai_api_key&quot;\n</code></pre>\n<p>The chart renders these into the <code>[secrets.refs]</code> section of the generated <code>config.toml</code>.</p>\n<p>For AWS, the chart should include a <code>ServiceAccount</code> annotation for IRSA:</p>\n<pre><code class=\"language-yaml\">serviceAccount:\n  annotations:\n    eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/openab-secrets-reader\n</code></pre>\n<hr />\n<h2>6. Examples</h2>\n<h3>Minimal: AWS Secrets Manager on EKS</h3>\n<pre><code class=\"language-toml\">[secrets.refs]\ndiscord_token = &quot;aws-sm://openab/prod#discord_bot_token&quot;\nopenai_key    = &quot;aws-sm://openab/prod#openai_api_key&quot;\n\n[discord]\nbot_token = &quot;${secrets.discord_token}&quot;\n</code></pre>\n<p>IAM policy on the pod's service account:</p>\n<pre><code class=\"language-json\">{\n  &quot;Effect&quot;: &quot;Allow&quot;,\n  &quot;Action&quot;: [&quot;secretsmanager:GetSecretValue&quot;],\n  &quot;Resource&quot;: &quot;arn:aws:secretsmanager:*:*:secret:openab/*&quot;\n}\n</code></pre>\n<h3>Medium: Exec with HashiCorp Vault CLI</h3>\n<p>Pre-boot hook downloads the script:</p>\n<pre><code class=\"language-toml\">[hooks.pre_boot]\ninline = '''\n#!/bin/sh\nvault login -method=kubernetes role=openab &gt; /dev/null\n'''\n\n[secrets.refs]\ndb_password = &quot;exec:///home/agent/.local/bin/vault-get.sh secret/openab db_password&quot;\n</code></pre>\n<p>Where <code>vault-get.sh</code>:</p>\n<pre><code class=\"language-bash\">#!/bin/sh\n# Usage: vault-get.sh &lt;path&gt; &lt;key&gt;\nvault kv get -field=&quot;$2&quot; &quot;$1&quot;\n</code></pre>\n<h3>Advanced: Mixed providers</h3>\n<pre><code class=\"language-toml\">[hooks.pre_boot]\nscript = &quot;/etc/openab/pre-boot.sh&quot;\n\n[secrets.refs]\n# AWS-managed secrets\ndiscord_token = &quot;aws-sm://openab/prod#discord_bot_token&quot;\n# Vault-managed secrets via exec\ngithub_pat    = &quot;exec:///home/agent/.local/bin/get-secret.sh vault/openab github_pat&quot;\n\n[secrets.aws]\nregion = &quot;ap-northeast-1&quot;\n\n[secrets.exec]\ntimeout_seconds = 15\n</code></pre>\n",
      "data": {
        "title": "ADR: Secrets Management"
      }
    },
    {
      "slug": "adr/telegram-rich-messages",
      "html": "<h1>ADR: Telegram Rich Messages Support</h1>\n<p><strong>Status:</strong> Accepted<br />\n<strong>Date:</strong> 2026-06-14<br />\n<strong>Author:</strong> 超渡法師<br />\n<strong>Bot API Version:</strong> 10.1 (June 11, 2026)</p>\n<h2>Context</h2>\n<p>Telegram Bot API 10.1 introduced <strong>Rich Messages</strong> — a structured formatting system that allows bots to send highly formatted content (headings, tables, code blocks, collages, math formulas, etc.) and <strong>stream AI-generated replies</strong> with seamless rich formatting.</p>\n<p>Currently, the OAB Telegram adapter in <code>gateway/src/adapters/telegram.rs</code> uses <code>sendMessage</code> with <code>parse_mode: Markdown</code> for all replies. This limits formatting to basic inline styles and lacks support for tables and headings.</p>\n<h2>Decision</h2>\n<p>Add Rich Message support to the Telegram gateway adapter with three capabilities:</p>\n<h3>1. <code>sendRichMessage</code> for structured replies</h3>\n<p>When the agent output contains complex formatting (tables, headings, long-form content), use <code>sendRichMessage</code> with <code>InputRichMessage.markdown</code> instead of <code>sendMessage</code>.</p>\n<h3>2. <code>sendRichMessageDraft</code> for AI streaming</h3>\n<p>Implement streaming UX via the draft → final pattern:</p>\n<pre><code>sendRichMessageDraft(draft_id=N, rich_message={markdown: partial})  // updates animate\n   ... repeat as content grows ...\nsendRichMessage(rich_message={markdown: final})                     // persist\n</code></pre>\n<h3>3. <code>editMessageText</code> with <code>rich_message</code> param</h3>\n<p>For editing existing rich messages (e.g., updating a streaming reply).</p>\n<h2>Architecture</h2>\n<pre><code>Agent output (markdown)\n       │\n       ▼\n┌─────────────────────────────┐\n│  TG Adapter (gateway)       │\n│                             │\n│  classify_reply(content) →  │\n│    Simple  → sendMessage    │\n│    Complex → sendRichMessage│\n│    Stream  → Draft → Final  │\n└─────────────────────────────┘\n</code></pre>\n<h3>Classification heuristic</h3>\n<p>A reply is &quot;complex&quot; if it contains any of:</p>\n<ul>\n<li>Markdown table (<code>|---|</code>)</li>\n<li>ATX headings (<code># </code>, <code>## </code>)</li>\n<li>Content &gt; 4096 chars (sendMessage limit)</li>\n</ul>\n<p>Code blocks (triple backtick) are intentionally <strong>not</strong> classified as complex — <code>sendMessage</code> preserves syntax highlighting with language headers and copy buttons, which <code>RichBlockPreformatted</code> currently lacks.</p>\n<p>Otherwise, fall back to <code>sendMessage</code> with <code>Markdown</code> parse mode for maximum client compatibility.</p>\n<h3>Rich Message Limits (from API docs)</h3>\n<table>\n<thead>\n<tr>\n<th>Limit</th>\n<th>Value</th>\n</tr>\n</thead>\n<tbody>\n<tr>\n<td>Text length</td>\n<td>32,768 UTF-8 chars</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Blocks</td>\n<td>500</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Nesting</td>\n<td>16 levels</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Media</td>\n<td>50 attachments</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Table columns</td>\n<td>20</td>\n</tr>\n</tbody>\n</table>\n<h2>Implementation Plan</h2>\n<h3>Phase 1: <code>sendRichMessage</code> (basic)</h3>\n<ul>\n<li>Add <code>send_rich_message()</code> function to <code>telegram.rs</code></li>\n<li>Add classification logic in <code>handle_reply()</code></li>\n<li>Pass markdown directly to <code>InputRichMessage.markdown</code> (no conversion needed — Rich Markdown is GitHub Flavored Markdown compatible)</li>\n</ul>\n<h3>Phase 2: Streaming via <code>sendRichMessageDraft</code></h3>\n<ul>\n<li>Add <code>send_rich_message_draft()</code> function</li>\n<li>Integrate with existing gateway streaming infrastructure</li>\n<li>Use <code>RichBlockThinking</code> for &quot;thinking&quot; animation during agent processing</li>\n</ul>\n<h3>Phase 3: Fallback &amp; compatibility</h3>\n<ul>\n<li>Detect API errors (old clients / bot API version mismatch) and fall back to <code>sendMessage</code></li>\n<li>Feature-gate behind env var: <code>TELEGRAM_RICH_MESSAGES=true</code> (default on, set <code>=false</code> to opt out)</li>\n</ul>\n<h2>Consequences</h2>\n<p><strong>Positive:</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li>Much better formatting for PR reviews, code analysis, structured reports</li>\n<li>Native streaming UX for AI responses (no more &quot;typing...&quot; placeholder)</li>\n<li>No conversion layer needed — agent markdown passes through directly</li>\n</ul>\n<p><strong>Negative:</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li>Requires Bot API 10.1+ (June 2026) — older Telegram clients may not render correctly</li>\n<li>Two code paths to maintain (sendMessage vs sendRichMessage)</li>\n</ul>\n<h2>References</h2>\n<ul>\n<li><a href=\"https://core.telegram.org/bots/api#june-11-2026\">Bot API 10.1 Changelog</a></li>\n<li><a href=\"https://core.telegram.org/bots/api#rich-message-formatting-options\">Rich Message Formatting Options</a></li>\n<li><a href=\"https://core.telegram.org/bots/api#sendrichmessage\">sendRichMessage</a></li>\n<li><a href=\"https://core.telegram.org/bots/api#sendrichmessagedraft\">sendRichMessageDraft</a></li>\n</ul>\n",
      "data": {
        "title": "ADR: Telegram Rich Messages Support"
      }
    },

      "slug": "adr/turn-boundary-batching",
      "html": "<h1>ADR: Turn-Boundary Message Batching</h1>\n<ul>\n<li><strong>Status:</strong> Proposed</li>\n<li><strong>Date:</strong> 2026-04-29</li>\n<li><strong>Author:</strong> @brettchien</li>\n<li><strong>Tracking issue:</strong> <a href=\"https://github.com/openabdev/openab/issues/580\">#580</a> — kept as historical discussion record</li>\n<li><strong>Implementation PR:</strong> <a href=\"https://github.com/openabdev/openab/pull/686\">#686</a> (Phase 1 wiring; the ADR documents the design that PR implements)</li>\n<li><strong>Related:</strong> <a href=\"https://github.com/openabdev/openab/issues/78\">#78</a> (Session Management — precondition), <a href=\"https://github.com/openabdev/openab/issues/58\">#58</a> (per-connection locking — precondition), <a href=\"https://github.com/openabdev/openab/issues/307\">#307</a> (cross-session blocking — adjacent symptom of §2.7)</li>\n<li><strong>Anchor pinning:</strong>\n<ul>\n<li><strong>Released-code anchors (file:line) — pinned to v0.8.2-beta.1</strong> (<a href=\"https://github.com/openabdev/openab/commit/52052b8b104a85a7073dd6ae99eeb9f2fd331abe\"><code>52052b8</code></a>). All <code>acp/connection.rs:NNN</code>, <code>acp/pool.rs:NNN</code>, <code>adapter.rs:NNN</code>, <code>discord.rs:NNN</code>, <code>slack.rs:NNN</code> references resolve at this SHA. They will drift against later commits — that's expected; the ADR documents the <em>design</em> relative to a stable base, not a moving target.</li>\n<li><strong>New modules (e.g. <code>src/dispatch.rs</code>) — described conceptually</strong>, no line numbers, since they do not exist at v0.8.2-beta.1.</li>\n<li><strong>Implementation cross-check anchor.</strong> Conceptual descriptions of new code are validated against <a href=\"https://github.com/openabdev/openab/tree/e119abf62b0ee97241e896000509ef4436f6574e\"><code>feature/turn-boundary-batching-v2</code> @ <code>e119abf</code></a> (PR #686 head at v0.6 of this ADR). When the PR's design <em>contract</em> changes (struct shape, function signature, error semantics), the ADR is updated and the changelog notes the new cross-check SHA. When the PR only refactors internals without contract changes, the ADR stays put.</li>\n</ul>\n</li>\n</ul>\n<hr />\n<h2>1. Context</h2>\n<h3>1.1 Problem</h3>\n<p>Within one thread, openab today processes one user message per ACP turn. After RFC #78 §2b each thread has its own <code>Arc&lt;Mutex&lt;AcpConnection&gt;&gt;</code> (<code>acp/pool.rs:15</code>), so inter-thread isolation is solved — but <strong>inside one thread</strong>, messages that arrive while a turn is running become independent <code>tokio::spawn</code> tasks racing for the per-connection mutex (<code>discord.rs:600-608</code>), each ending up dispatched as a separate sequential ACP turn.</p>\n<p><code>adapter.rs:254</code> → <code>pool.with_connection(thread_key, |conn| { ... })</code> (<code>acp/pool.rs:223</code>) calls <code>conn.session_prompt(content_blocks).await</code> (<code>adapter.rs:260</code>) exactly once per call. <code>content_blocks</code> is built from one user message — its prompt text plus that message's own image / transcript blocks (<code>adapter.rs:156-172</code>). Multiple <code>ContentBlock</code>s in one turn means &quot;one message with multiple media parts,&quot; never &quot;multiple messages.&quot;</p>\n<p>Tokio's <code>Mutex</code> keeps a fair-ish FIFO <code>LinkedList&lt;Waker&gt;</code> but <a href=\"https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/sync/struct.Mutex.html\">does not guarantee strict FIFO</a>; the mutex only sees &quot;someone is waiting&quot; — wakers are opaque, so it cannot enumerate pending messages, inspect content, or batch them. Batching therefore can't be retrofitted onto the mutex; it requires an explicit queue at a layer that owns the message data.</p>\n<p>Three workload patterns this hurts:</p>\n<ol>\n<li><strong>Stream-of-thought split</strong> — <code>&quot;can you check the build&quot;</code> → <code>&quot;actually wait&quot;</code> → <code>&quot;check the build *and* run the e2e tests&quot;</code> in 5 seconds. Today: 3 sequential turns; turn 1 wastes work, turn 2 reacts before seeing the correction, turn 3 finally has the full intent.</li>\n<li><strong>Late attachment / clarification</strong> — text question, then 8 seconds later the screenshot. Today: 2 turns, the first answers without the screenshot.</li>\n<li><strong>Independent topics interleaved</strong> — two unrelated asks back-to-back. The broker should merge them into one ACP turn; the agent answers both in one response (agents handle multi-intent prompts well).</li>\n</ol>\n<h3>1.2 Why at the broker layer</h3>\n<p>ACP coding CLIs — Claude Code, Cursor, Codex — consume one turn at a time: each <code>session_prompt</code> is one input → one response. They do not inspect incoming chat traffic and do not batch messages themselves. Adapter-level pre-turn debouncing (e.g. Hermes' <code>_pending_text_batches</code>) imposes a latency floor on every message including isolated ones, which conflicts with the zero-latency-first-message goal. The broker is the only layer that can buffer <em>during</em> an in-flight turn (when the user is already waiting on the agent) and dispatch at turn completion, paying zero added latency for the first message and amortizing nothing for subsequent ones.</p>\n<p>Per-thread scope is required because conversation scope in openab = thread; per-thread keying matches the existing <code>Arc&lt;Mutex&lt;AcpConnection&gt;&gt;</code> keying (<code>adapter.rs:173-180</code>). Per-channel or global merging would conflate independent conversations.</p>\n<h3>1.3 Goals &amp; non-goals</h3>\n<p><strong>Goals:</strong> replace <strong>1 message → 1 turn</strong> with <strong>N messages-arrived-during-turn → 1 next turn</strong> within a single thread; introduce the data structure required (a per-thread bounded <code>mpsc::channel</code>); achieve deterministic same-thread ordering as a side benefit.</p>\n<p><strong>Non-goals:</strong></p>\n<table>\n<thead>\n<tr>\n<th>Concern</th>\n<th>Layer that owns it</th>\n</tr>\n</thead>\n<tbody>\n<tr>\n<td>Inter-thread isolation</td>\n<td>Per-connection mutex (RFC #78 §2b / #58). Precondition.</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Cross-session blocking (#307)</td>\n<td>Different layer — about a <em>new</em> thread's session unable to start.</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Pre-turn debouncing</td>\n<td>Rejected; see §5.1.</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Topic detection / semantic grouping</td>\n<td>Deferred to ACP agent (it has the context and inference budget).</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Cancelling / restarting in-flight turns</td>\n<td>Existing <code>/cancel</code> semantics unchanged. <code>/cancel-all</code> covers buffered-message drop (Phase 1, §4.4).</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Persisting buffer across pod restarts</td>\n<td>Buffer only exists during in-flight turn — restart loses the in-flight turn anyway, so buffered messages share its fate.</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Replacing the per-connection mutex</td>\n<td>Mutex stays exactly as RFC #78 §2b describes it.</td>\n</tr>\n</tbody>\n</table>\n<hr />\n<h2>2. Mechanism Decision</h2>\n<p><strong>Decision:</strong> introduce a per-thread bounded <code>mpsc::channel</code> plus a long-lived consumer task. The producer (platform event loop) sends each arrival into the channel via <code>Dispatcher::submit</code>. The consumer drains greedily at turn boundaries and dispatches the batch as <strong>one</strong> ACP <code>session_prompt</code> call. The packing of those N arrival events into <code>Vec&lt;ContentBlock&gt;</code> is specified in §3.</p>\n<h3>2.1 Three invariants</h3>\n<p>The design rests on three structural invariants. All later choices in §2 and §3 are concrete instances of one of these.</p>\n<p><strong>I1 — First message after idle has zero added latency.</strong> The first arrival on an idle thread fires immediately. The buffer only fills <em>during an active turn</em>, when the user is already waiting on the agent. The agent's turn duration is itself a natural &quot;user is waiting&quot; window, used for free.</p>\n<p><strong>I2 — At most one in-flight turn per thread.</strong> All buffering happens between turns, never within. The per-connection mutex plus the per-thread consumer task together enforce this — the consumer drains, fires <code>session_prompt</code>, awaits completion, then loops back to <code>recv</code>. No two <code>session_prompt</code> calls overlap on the same thread.</p>\n<p><strong>I3 — Broker structural fidelity (top-level invariant).</strong></p>\n<blockquote>\n<p>The broker must faithfully preserve structural attribution: each chat-history arrival event (its sender, its text, its attachments) appears in the dispatched batch exactly as received — no merging, no splitting, no reordering, no attachment re-attribution, no heuristic pairing of related-looking messages, no semantic directives injected to instruct the agent how to interpret the input.</p>\n</blockquote>\n<p>The broker is a transparent buffer that extends the existing per-arrival-event template (<code>&lt;sender_context&gt;...&lt;/sender_context&gt;\\n\\n{prompt}</code>, <code>adapter.rs:156-172</code>). <code>{prompt}</code> is placed verbatim — broker never parses or transforms its content. Every dispatch — <code>per-message</code>, <code>per-thread</code>, or <code>per-lane</code> — is just N repetitions of that template concatenated; for <code>per-message</code> mode N is always 1.</p>\n<p>I3 is load-bearing for §3 (packing) and §6.4 (compliance rules). Every transformation the broker would apply is information the ACP agent can no longer recover; the rule is &quot;must not&quot;, not &quot;should not&quot;.</p>\n<h3>2.2 Architecture</h3>\n<pre><code>state                    event                              action\n────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────\nthread idle              M1 arrives                          fire turn 1 with M1 immediately\nturn 1 in flight         M2 arrives                          send M2 into channel\nturn 1 in flight         M3 arrives                          send M3 into channel\nturn 1 completes         (consumer recv wakes)               drain channel → fire turn 2 with [M2, M3]\nturn 2 in flight         M4 arrives                          send M4 into channel\nturn 2 completes         (consumer recv wakes)               drain channel → fire turn 3 with [M4]\nturn 3 completes         (channel empty)                     consumer parks on recv → awaits next message\n</code></pre>\n<pre><code>┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐\n│ Platform event loop (Discord / Slack / Gateway adapter)         │\n│  inbound msg ──gates (allow_*, bot_turns, mentions)──▶           │\n└────────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┘\n                                     │  (per-message tokio::spawn)\n                                     ▼\n                          ┌────────────────────────┐\n                          │   Dispatcher           │\n                          │   per_thread:          │\n                          │   HashMap&lt;key, Handle&gt; │   ◀── std::sync::Mutex (§2.5)\n                          │   (lazy insert)        │\n                          └─────────┬──────────────┘\n                                    │  tx.send(BufferedMessage).await\n                                    ▼\n   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐\n   │ ThreadHandle (one per active thread):                        │\n   │   tx: mpsc::Sender&lt;BufferedMessage&gt;      (cap = max_buffered)│\n   │   _consumer: JoinHandle (consumer_loop task)                 │\n   │   generation: u64                                            │\n   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘\n                                    │\n                                    ▼\n   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐\n   │ consumer_loop (one per active thread):                       │\n   │   loop {                                                     │\n   │     first = rx.recv().await       // I1: 1st msg has 0 latency│\n   │     batch = greedy_drain(first, max_buffered, max_tokens)    │\n   │     dispatch_batch(...)           // pack (§3) + session_prompt│\n   │   }                                                          │\n   └────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────┘\n                        │  pool.with_connection(thread_key, ...)\n                        ▼\n   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐\n   │ SessionPool / AcpConnection (unchanged from v0.8.2-beta.1)   │\n   │   conn.session_prompt(Vec&lt;ContentBlock&gt;).await               │\n   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘\n</code></pre>\n<p>The <code>Dispatcher</code> sits <strong>above</strong> <code>SessionPool</code> in the call graph. Per-thread keying matches the existing <code>thread_id</code> keying from <code>acp/pool.rs:15</code>. The per-connection mutex still wraps each ACP turn but no longer determines message order — ordering moves to the per-thread mpsc enqueue (μs-scale handle lookup) instead of the per-connection mutex's waker list (held during the 30s+ ACP turn).</p>\n<p><strong>Wiring (Phase 1, Discord + Slack + Gateway — see §4.4):</strong></p>\n<pre><code class=\"language-rust\">// At v0.8.2-beta.1 (discord.rs:600-608):\ntokio::spawn(async move { router.handle_message(...).await });\n\n// After Phase 1 — all three modes go through the same dispatcher; the mode\n// only changes (cap, grouping, idle_timeout). The dispatcher's `key()`\n// computes the mpsc identity from grouping; `Per-Message` reduces to a\n// 1-deep buffer per thread (each message dispatches alone, FIFO).\ntokio::spawn(async move {\n    // `buf` carries `other_bot_present: bool` (§2.6) — no separate parameter.\n    dispatcher.submit(thread_key, thread_channel, adapter, buf).await\n});\n\n// where (cap, grouping, idle) are derived from message_processing_mode:\n//   PerMessage -&gt; (1,                   Thread, PER_MESSAGE_CONSUMER_IDLE_TIMEOUT)\n//   PerThread  -&gt; (max_buffered_messages, Thread, DEFAULT_CONSUMER_IDLE_TIMEOUT)\n//   PerLane    -&gt; (max_buffered_messages, Lane,   DEFAULT_CONSUMER_IDLE_TIMEOUT)\n</code></pre>\n<p><code>PerMessage</code> is structurally a uniform-path special case (cap=1; consumer drains exactly one message per turn). <code>PerThread</code> and <code>PerLane</code> differ only in dispatcher key shape — <code>PerThread</code> keys mpsc identity by <code>(platform, thread_id)</code>, <code>PerLane</code> keys by <code>(platform, thread_id, sender_id)</code> so each sender owns a separate buffer + consumer (still serialized through the shared <code>Arc&lt;Mutex&lt;AcpConnection&gt;&gt;</code> per thread). See §4.1 for config-side rationale.</p>\n<h3>2.3 Producer / consumer lifecycle</h3>\n<p>Each active thread owns a bounded <code>mpsc::channel</code> (capacity = <code>max_buffered_messages</code> from config) and a long-lived consumer task that drains it. The struct shape:</p>\n<pre><code class=\"language-rust\">struct BufferedMessage {\n    prompt: String,\n    extra_blocks: Vec&lt;ContentBlock&gt;,\n    sender_json: String,            // serialized SenderContext (see §3.2)\n    trigger_msg: MessageRef,        // anchor for reactions\n    arrived_at: Instant,\n    sender_name: String,            // display name (not a stable user ID)\n    estimated_tokens: usize,        // for max_batch_tokens cap (§4.3)\n    other_bot_present: bool,        // freshness snapshot, read from batch.last() at dispatch (§2.6)\n}\n\nstruct ThreadHandle {\n    tx: mpsc::Sender&lt;BufferedMessage&gt;,\n    _consumer: tokio::task::JoinHandle&lt;()&gt;,\n    generation: u64,                // race-safe eviction (§2.5)\n    channel_id: String,             // for shutdown logging (§6.6)\n    adapter_kind: String,           // &quot;discord&quot; / &quot;slack&quot; / &quot;gateway&quot;\n}\n\npub struct Dispatcher {\n    per_thread: std::sync::Mutex&lt;HashMap&lt;String, ThreadHandle&gt;&gt;,\n    target: Arc&lt;dyn DispatchTarget&gt;,\n    max_buffered_messages: usize,\n    max_batch_tokens: usize,\n    idle_timeout: Duration,         // per-mode (§6.10)\n    // No Arc&lt;AtomicBool&gt; for other_bot_present — the bool snapshot rides on each\n    // BufferedMessage and the consumer reads batch.last()'s value at dispatch (§2.6).\n}\n</code></pre>\n<p><strong><code>submit(thread_key, thread_channel, adapter, msg)</code></strong> (called from the platform event loop's per-message <code>tokio::spawn</code>'d task; the per-message <code>other_bot_present</code> is carried inside <code>msg</code>):</p>\n<ol>\n<li>Lock <code>per_thread</code>; lazily construct the <code>ThreadHandle</code> if absent — creates <code>mpsc::channel(max_buffered_messages)</code>, spawns the consumer task with the dispatcher's per-mode <code>idle_timeout</code>, initialises <code>generation = 0</code>; release the lock. On SendError eviction (§2.5), the replacement handle gets <code>generation = old + 1</code>.</li>\n<li><code>tx.send(msg).await</code> — returns immediately if the channel has space; <strong>parks the calling task if the channel is full</strong>. Only this <code>submit</code> future blocks; the platform event loop is unaffected because <code>submit</code> runs inside its own <code>tokio::spawn</code>'d task per inbound message.</li>\n<li>On <code>SendError</code> (consumer task has died): see §2.5.</li>\n</ol>\n<p><strong><code>consumer_loop(thread_key)</code></strong> (one per active thread, lives until the channel closes):</p>\n<ol>\n<li><code>let first = rx.recv().await</code> — blocks until at least one message arrives. (I1: zero latency on first message after idle.)</li>\n<li><strong>Greedy drain</strong> with two stop conditions:\n<ul>\n<li><code>batch.len() == max_buffered_messages</code>, or</li>\n<li><code>cumulative_tokens + next.estimated_tokens &gt; max_batch_tokens</code> (soft cap, §4.3).</li>\n</ul>\n</li>\n<li><strong>Read freshness inputs at dispatch time</strong> — pull <code>other_bot_present</code> from the <em>last</em> message in the drained batch (<code>batch.last().unwrap().other_bot_present</code>); the snapshot rides on <code>BufferedMessage</code> (§2.6).</li>\n<li>Dispatch as <strong>one ACP turn</strong> via <code>dispatch_batch</code> — which applies 👀 reactions to all batch messages (§6.7), packs via <code>pack_arrival_event</code> (§3), then calls <code>pool.with_connection</code> + <code>session_prompt</code>.</li>\n<li>Loop back to step 1.</li>\n</ol>\n<p><strong>Idle eviction:</strong> the dispatcher tracks its own per-mode <code>idle_timeout</code> (§6.10) — <code>PER_MESSAGE_CONSUMER_IDLE_TIMEOUT = 10s</code> for <code>per-message</code>, <code>DEFAULT_CONSUMER_IDLE_TIMEOUT = 300s</code> for <code>per-thread</code> / <code>per-lane</code>. The consumer self-evicts on lazy timeout (<code>recv</code> returns <code>None</code> after the deadline elapses while parked); <code>Dispatcher::sweep_stale</code> (called periodically from <code>main.rs</code>) evicts consumers that never wake up to self-evict — required for one-shot threads where the user sends one message and never returns. Either path drops the <code>ThreadHandle</code> → <code>Sender</code> drops → channel closes → <code>recv()</code> returns <code>None</code> → consumer exits cleanly. No leader-election race; there is always exactly one consumer per active thread. Independent of the connection pool's <code>cleanup_idle</code> (<code>acp/pool.rs:295</code>), which keys on <code>AcpConnection.last_active</code> and is unchanged by this ADR.</p>\n<h3>2.4 Producer-side gating (multi-party)</h3>\n<p><strong>Buffer invariant: by the time a message reaches the buffer, it has already been determined to be intended for our agent.</strong> All multi-party complexity lives upstream of <code>submit</code>:</p>\n<table>\n<thead>\n<tr>\n<th>Gate</th>\n<th>Source</th>\n<th>Multi-party role</th>\n</tr>\n</thead>\n<tbody>\n<tr>\n<td><code>allow_bot_messages</code> (off / mentions / all)</td>\n<td><code>slack.rs:710-765</code></td>\n<td>Whether bot messages enter at all.</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td><code>allow_user_messages</code> (involved / mentions / multibot-mentions)</td>\n<td><code>slack.rs:768-810</code></td>\n<td>Which human messages we respond to.</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td><code>trusted_bot_ids</code></td>\n<td>config</td>\n<td>Whitelist for <code>mentions</code> / <code>all</code> modes.</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td><code>bot_turns</code> consecutive-bot limit</td>\n<td><code>slack.rs:672-696</code></td>\n<td>Loop guard. <strong>Per-message at ingest, not per batch.</strong></td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Eager multi-bot detection</td>\n<td><code>slack.rs:649-657</code></td>\n<td>Sets <code>other_bot_present</code> → triggers <code>multibot-mentions</code> semantics.</td>\n</tr>\n</tbody>\n</table>\n<p>Implications for the dispatcher:</p>\n<ul>\n<li><code>other_bot_present</code> is a per-thread fact set upstream; each <code>BufferedMessage</code> carries the bool snapshot, and the consumer reads <code>batch.last().other_bot_present</code> at dispatch time (§2.6).</li>\n<li><code>MAX_CONSECUTIVE_BOT_TURNS</code> runs <em>before</em> <code>submit</code>; batching is downstream and cannot bypass it. Bot-turn-limit counts batches as turns (one ACP invocation = one logical turn); the per-message ingest counter is unchanged.</li>\n<li>Per-sub-message attribution in a batch is carried by repeated standalone <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> delimiter blocks (§3).</li>\n</ul>\n<h3>2.5 Error handling on consumer death</h3>\n<p><strong><code>SendError</code> is a real surface introduced by the per-thread-consumer architecture</strong> — <code>tx.send().await</code> returns <code>Err</code> only when the receiver half is dropped, which happens when the consumer task exits (idle timeout — §6.10; panic inside <code>dispatch_batch</code> or its callees; process tear-down). v0.8.2-beta.1's per-message direct-dispatch has no analogous failure mode.</p>\n<p><strong>Decision: transparent retry once, surface only if retry also fails.</strong> The handler:</p>\n<ol>\n<li><strong>Proactive <code>is_finished</code> check at submit head.</strong> Before consulting the entry, <code>submit</code> peeks at the existing <code>ThreadHandle</code> and removes it if <code>consumer.is_finished()</code> returned true — this is the common case (idle-timeout exit observed by the producer first), and it converts what would have been a <code>SendError</code> round-trip into a normal lazy-insert. Stale entries don't accumulate either.</li>\n<li><strong>On <code>SendError</code> (the race window past the proactive check):</strong> evict under lock with the generation guard (race-safe, see below), then <em>transparently</em> spawn a fresh consumer and re-send the same <code>BufferedMessage</code> once. No user-visible signal on the happy path.</li>\n<li><strong>If the retry also fails:</strong> evict the retry handle, then ❌ on <code>msg.trigger_msg</code> via <code>adapter.add_reaction(..., emojis.error)</code>, ⚠️ via <code>adapter.send_message(thread_channel, format!(&quot;⚠️ {}&quot;, format_user_error(&quot;dispatch consumer exited unexpectedly&quot;)))</code>, and <code>return Err(DispatchError::ConsumerDead)</code>. The shape mirrors <code>stream_prompt</code>'s Err handler in <code>handle_message</code> (<code>adapter.rs:212-234</code>: <code>set_error()</code> + ⚠️ + return <code>Err</code>).</li>\n</ol>\n<p><strong>Why retry once.</strong> The dominant <code>SendError</code> path is the <em>first-message-after-idle</em> race: the consumer's idle timer fired and the task is in the process of exiting, but the producer didn't observe <code>is_finished()</code> in time. Surfacing that to the user as ❌ + ⚠️ would be wrong — there's no real failure, just a benign window. Retrying once with a fresh consumer closes the race without complicating user expectations. If the retry <em>also</em> fails, that's a genuine bug (panic inside <code>dispatch_batch</code>, runtime tear-down) and surfacing it is correct.</p>\n<p><strong>Why both signals on the failing path.</strong> ❌ on <code>msg.trigger_msg</code> answers <em>&quot;which message failed?&quot;</em> (anchored to a specific message ID, survives scrolling). The <code>⚠️</code> text answers <em>&quot;why did it fail / what should I do?&quot;</em>. In per-message dispatch they were partly redundant; in batched dispatch with rapid-fire M1/M2/M3 each carries distinct load.</p>\n<p><strong>Why bounded to one retry — three reasons converge:</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li><strong>No spin-loop possible.</strong> Retry is unconditionally bounded to a single attempt; &quot;<code>SendError → evict → retry</code> on permanently broken stdio&quot; cannot materialize.</li>\n<li><strong><code>SendError</code> past the retry is informative.</strong> If the second attempt also dies, it's a real bug. Surface and log is the right response.</li>\n<li><strong>Consistency on the failing path.</strong> Released code's contract is &quot;if dispatch fails, you see <code>⚠️</code> and re-send if you still want.&quot; The dispatcher inherits that contract for the truly-broken case while transparently absorbing the benign idle-race case.</li>\n</ul>\n<p><strong>Race-safe eviction.</strong> Two <code>submit</code> calls can observe <code>SendError</code> on the same handle concurrently. Eviction happens under the <code>per_thread</code> lock with the <code>generation: u64</code> counter on <code>ThreadHandle</code> — only the first observer evicts (<code>try_evict_locked</code> no-ops if the captured generation no longer matches the map entry). The second observer takes the lock and either (a) finds the entry gone, or (b) finds it already replaced by a fresher consumer (newer generation); both observers then proceed to the retry-spawn-or-reuse step, which is itself an <code>entry().or_insert_with</code> under the same lock, so concurrent retries collapse onto the same fresh <code>ThreadHandle</code>. If both retries succeed, neither surfaces a user-visible signal; if both retries fail (genuine bug, e.g. persistent panic source), each observer reacts on its <em>own</em> <code>msg.trigger_msg</code> and emits its <em>own</em> <code>⚠️</code> text — no cross-attribution.</p>\n<p><strong><code>per_thread</code> uses <code>std::sync::Mutex</code>, not <code>tokio::Mutex</code>.</strong> The critical section is a synchronous <code>HashMap</code> get/insert/remove with no <code>.await</code> inside; the async-machinery cost of <code>tokio::Mutex</code> buys nothing. <code>generation: u64</code> is plain (not atomic) because every read and write happens inside the <code>per_thread</code> lock — the surrounding mutex provides ordering.</p>\n<p><strong>Disjoint from <code>/cancel-all</code></strong> (§4.4). <code>cancel_buffered_thread</code> removes the handle from <code>per_thread</code> <em>before</em> aborting the consumer, so any <em>fresh</em> <code>submit</code> arriving after lands on the lazily-constructed new handle — no <code>SendError</code> on that path. Producers already parked in <code>tx.send().await</code> wake with <code>Err</code> and enter the SendError → retry path; the retry's <code>or_insert_with</code> constructs a fresh consumer (the cancel removed the old entry), and the retry succeeds.</p>\n<p><strong><code>/cancel-all</code> race with concurrent <code>submit</code> is intentional.</strong> If a <code>submit</code> arrives in the window between <code>cancel_buffered_thread</code> removing the old handle and the next <code>submit</code> constructing a new one, that new <code>submit</code> creates a fresh consumer via the normal lazy-insert path. This is by design: <code>cancel_buffered_thread</code> clears only the messages buffered at cancel time; messages that arrive after the cancel are treated as a fresh conversation start.</p>\n<p><strong>Residual losses (same shape as a pod restart mid-turn):</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li><strong>In-flight batch in the dead consumer's frame.</strong> Lost when the panic unwinds. These messages can't be reacted from the SendError path because their <code>submit</code> already returned <code>Ok</code> before the consumer died.</li>\n<li><strong>Already-enqueued mpsc messages</strong> (in the queue but not yet drained). Lost when <code>Receiver</code> drops.</li>\n</ul>\n<p>A future supervisor catching consumer-task panic could iterate the in-flight batch and react ❌ on each; out of Phase 1 scope.</p>\n<h3>2.6 <code>other_bot_present</code> freshness</h3>\n<p><strong>Required invariant:</strong> the dispatcher must read approximately-dispatch-time state, not consumer-spawn-time state.
