If a new bot joins the thread mid-conversation, a stale reading misclassifies the batch's addressee semantics.</p>\n<p><strong>Mechanism.</strong> Each <code>BufferedMessage</code> carries an <code>other_bot_present: bool</code> snapshot captured at submit time, alongside its <code>prompt</code> and <code>extra_blocks</code>. At dispatch time the consumer reads the snapshot from the <em>last</em> message in the drained batch (<code>batch.last().unwrap().other_bot_present</code>) — i.e. the freshest reading available to the dispatcher.</p>\n<p><strong>Why per-message snapshot, not <code>Arc&lt;AtomicBool&gt;</code> mirror.</strong> An earlier draft of this ADR specified a Dispatcher-owned <code>Arc&lt;AtomicBool&gt;</code> mirror written by the producer's early-detect path (<code>slack.rs:649-657</code>, Discord analog) and read by the consumer immediately before each <code>dispatch_batch</code>. The implementation took the simpler route: pass the <code>bool</code> through <code>BufferedMessage</code> and read the last one. Trade-offs:</p>\n<ul>\n<li><strong>Staleness bound.</strong> With the mirror, the consumer always sees the live producer state at dispatch time. With the snapshot, freshness is bounded by the time between the last message's <code>submit</code> and the consumer's drain — at most one mpsc round-trip plus the batch's own <code>try_recv</code> slack (μs to low-ms). For the misclassification this invariant guards against (a peer bot joins mid-conversation), this bound is well within the time scale that matters.</li>\n<li><strong>Coupling.</strong> The mirror approach requires the dispatcher to own a per-thread <code>Arc&lt;AtomicBool&gt;</code> and the producer to find and update it on every detect-update; the snapshot approach reuses the same producer code that would have updated the mirror, just feeding the value through <code>BufferedMessage</code> instead. Fewer moving parts.</li>\n</ul>\n<p>If staleness ever surfaces as a real bug, the mirror remains the upgrade path — <code>BufferedMessage.other_bot_present</code> is then read for <em>coarse</em> freshness and the mirror is consulted as a tiebreaker. Phase 1 keeps it simple.</p>\n<h3>2.7 <code>last_active</code> semantics — deferred</h3>\n<p><code>submit</code> does <strong>not</strong> touch <code>last_active</code>. The single <code>last_active: Instant</code> lives on <code>AcpConnection</code> (<code>acp/connection.rs:120</code>) and is touched at the start of <code>session_prompt()</code> (<code>acp/connection.rs:430</code>) and again on <code>prompt_done()</code> (<code>acp/connection.rs:468</code>); both run inside <code>stream_prompt</code>'s <code>pool.with_connection</code> lock guard. Batched dispatch preserves this exactly — the per-batch <code>session_prompt</code> call is the only liveness signal, just as in v0.8.2-beta.1.</p>\n<p><strong>Pre-existing concern (not closed by this ADR).</strong> The actual zombie mechanism in v0.8.2-beta.1 is not <code>last_active</code> staleness but <code>cleanup_idle</code>'s <code>try_lock</code> on the connection (<code>acp/pool.rs:312-313</code>, &quot;A busy session is not idle&quot;): the lock attempt sees the in-flight task holding the mutex while <code>await</code>-ing a hung ACP and skips the candidate before the predicate is even evaluated. The slot stays occupied until the ACP process is killed externally.</p>\n<p><strong>Two axes of impact:</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li><strong>Axis 1 — zombie's own lifetime (same across all three modes).</strong> The connection mutex is held by <code>stream_prompt.await</code> regardless of <code>MessageProcessingMode</code>; <code>cleanup_idle.try_lock</code> skips it identically; the slot stays occupied until the ACP process is killed externally or the holder task finally exits. Dispatch mode does not change this.</li>\n<li><strong>Axis 2 — user-visible blast radius (worse under <code>per-thread</code> / <code>per-lane</code>).</strong> In <code>per-message</code> mode, <code>submit</code> puts each arrival into a cap=1 buffer — the second user message after a hang immediately backpressures (or, if the previous message has cleared, blocks at the per-thread connection lock); the user sees &quot;no reply&quot; within seconds and stops sending. In <code>per-thread</code> / <code>per-lane</code> modes, <code>submit</code> returns <code>Ok</code> instantly while messages accumulate in the per-thread (or per-lane) mpsc buffer; the user keeps typing. When the consumer eventually dies (panic) or the <code>AcpConnection</code> is force-evicted, up to <code>max_buffered_messages</code> user messages can disappear at once per affected lane, versus ≤1 in <code>per-message</code> mode.</li>\n</ul>\n<p><strong>Existing related work — none of which closes this concern:</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li><strong>#309 / PR #310</strong> (closed 2026-04-13) — process-group kill + session suspend/resume. Fixes orphaned grandchildren after eviction but eviction still keys on the same single <code>last_active</code>.</li>\n<li><strong>#58</strong> (closed) — pool write-lock held during entire <code>stream_prompt</code>. Fixed via lock-granularity refactor; <code>last_active</code> semantics untouched.</li>\n<li><strong>#78</strong> (open RFC) — Session Management; §1b proposes <code>idle_timeout_minutes</code> vs <code>session_ttl_hours</code> split (duration-axis layering, not the indicator split needed here).</li>\n<li><strong>#307</strong> (open) — adjacent symptom of the same <code>try_lock</code> blocker; would partially benefit from a fix.</li>\n</ul>\n<p>The fix (indicator split + <code>cleanup_idle.try_lock</code> rework) is tracked in a dedicated follow-up issue, cross-referenced with #307. It is out of scope for this ADR because it touches <code>acp/pool.rs</code> eviction semantics independently of batching.</p>\n<h3>2.8 Benefits of N→1</h3>\n<p>Falling out of N-messages-into-1-turn (not the primary motivation, but real):</p>\n<p><strong>Token cost.</strong> Each ACP turn re-sends <code>system + tools + accumulated history + new input</code>. Three sequential turns:</p>\n<pre><code>T1 input  = sys + tools + M1\nT1 output = R1                       ← may be wasted\nT2 input  = sys + tools + M1 + R1 + M2\nT2 output = R2\nT3 input  = sys + tools + M1 + R1 + M2 + R2 + M3\nT3 output = R3\n</code></pre>\n<p>vs one batched turn: <code>input = sys + tools + [M1, M2, M3]</code>, output = single response. Saved tokens come from (in descending impact): wasted intermediate output, redundant tool invocations, intermediate responses re-fed, prompt-prefix cache invalidations.</p>\n<p><strong>Latency.</strong> Three sequential turns ≈ <code>T1 + T2 + T3</code> wall-clock; the batched path ≈ <code>T1 + T_batch</code> (M1 fires alone immediately; M2 and M3 merge into one follow-up turn). Leading-message latency is unchanged (I1).</p>\n<p><strong>Deterministic ordering.</strong> Same-thread ordering moves from approximate (<code>tokio::spawn</code> race + Tokio Mutex's not-strictly-FIFO waiter list, sync point held during 30s+ ACP turn) to strict (mpsc FIFO, sync point μs-scale on dispatcher mutex).</p>\n<p>These benefits scale with input fragmentation and do not apply to isolated messages (buffer never fills).</p>\n<hr />\n<h2>3. Packing Format Decision</h2>\n<p><strong>Decision:</strong> the broker emits <strong>N repetitions of the per-arrival-event template</strong> — a standalone <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;{json}&lt;/sender_context&gt;</code> Text block, followed by transcript Text blocks (if any), followed by <code>{prompt}</code> as its own Text block (omitted if empty), followed by non-Text attachments — concatenated into one <code>Vec&lt;ContentBlock&gt;</code>. <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> is its own ContentBlock and serves as a structural delimiter; the next opening of <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> ends the previous arrival event. One additive schema bump (<code>SenderContext.timestamp</code>, ISO 8601 UTC) makes adjacent same-author repetitions distinguishable.</p>\n<p>This subsumes T1.4 / B1 (attribution of attachments to their owning sub-message), T2.b (<code>sender_name</code> disambiguation — handled by the existing <code>sender_id</code> field), and T2.j (<code>arrived_at_relative</code> — agent computes from absolute timestamps).</p>\n<p>The chosen design preserves the existing per-arrival template from <code>adapter.rs:156-172</code>. Single-message dispatch differs from v0.8.2-beta.1 in three structural ways, all enumerated in §3.5: (1) <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> JSON gains an additive <code>timestamp</code> field; (2) <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> becomes its own ContentBlock instead of being prepended into the same Text block as <code>{prompt}</code>; (3) STT voice transcripts move from before the <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> envelope to inside the arrival event (after the delimiter, before <code>{prompt}</code>). Image ordering (after <code>{prompt}</code>) is unchanged. These changes apply uniformly across all three modes.</p>\n<h3>3.1 Per-arrival-event template</h3>\n<p>Per arrival event, <code>pack_arrival_event</code> emits this sequence of <code>ContentBlock</code>s:</p>\n<pre><code>ContentBlock::Text { &quot;&lt;sender_context&gt;\\n{json}\\n&lt;/sender_context&gt;&quot; }   ← standalone delimiter\n[ContentBlock::Text from extra_blocks — e.g. STT transcripts, in arrival order]\nContentBlock::Text { &quot;{prompt}&quot; }                                       ← omitted if {prompt} is empty\n[non-Text ContentBlocks from extra_blocks — e.g. ImageBlock, in arrival order]\n</code></pre>\n<p><code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> is its own block so that, in batched dispatch, agents can scan the <code>Vec&lt;ContentBlock&gt;</code> for <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> openers to find arrival boundaries without parsing inside any single Text block. Within an arrival, transcripts precede <code>{prompt}</code> (so voice content reads first, matching pre-batching adapter UX); images trail <code>{prompt}</code> (matching pre-batching adapter UX).</p>\n<p>For a single-message dispatch (<code>batch.len() == 1</code>) the minimum is two blocks: delimiter + prompt. Each transcript adds one Text block; each image adds one non-Text block. An empty-prompt arrival (e.g. voice-only) skips the prompt block — minimum becomes one delimiter + one transcript.</p>\n<p><code>{json}</code> is the existing <code>SenderContext</code> record:</p>\n<pre><code class=\"language-json\">{\n  &quot;schema&quot;: &quot;openab.sender.v1&quot;,\n  &quot;sender_id&quot;: &quot;…&quot;,\n  &quot;sender_name&quot;: &quot;…&quot;,\n  &quot;display_name&quot;: &quot;…&quot;,\n  &quot;channel&quot;: &quot;discord|slack|gateway&quot;,\n  &quot;channel_id&quot;: &quot;…&quot;,\n  &quot;is_bot&quot;: false,\n  &quot;timestamp&quot;: &quot;2026-04-27T06:13:17.927Z&quot;\n}\n</code></pre>\n<h3>3.2 <code>timestamp</code> additive field</h3>\n<p><code>SenderContext</code> JSON gains a <code>timestamp</code> field — ISO 8601 UTC, <strong>platform message creation time</strong> (not broker dispatch time):</p>\n<table>\n<thead>\n<tr>\n<th>Source</th>\n<th>Value</th>\n</tr>\n</thead>\n<tbody>\n<tr>\n<td>Discord adapter</td>\n<td><code>msg.timestamp</code> (serenity 0.12 <code>Timestamp</code>, RFC 3339 by default)</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Slack adapter</td>\n<td><code>slack_ts_to_iso8601(event.ts)</code> (proposed helper) — converts epoch-seconds-with-fractional to ISO 8601 with millisecond precision</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Gateway adapter</td>\n<td><code>chrono::Utc::now().to_rfc3339()</code> at receive time — best-effort for non-Discord/Slack channels; documented as approximate</td>\n</tr>\n</tbody>\n</table>\n<p><code>schema</code> stays <code>openab.sender.v1</code> — the field is additive and existing parsers keep working. Two purposes:</p>\n<ol>\n<li><strong>Distinguishability</strong> — adjacent same-author repetitions become structurally distinct even when other JSON fields would otherwise be byte-identical.</li>\n<li><strong>Subsumes <code>arrived_at_relative</code> (T2.j)</strong> — the agent computes any relative offset (typing cadence, rapid-fire vs slow correction) directly from absolute timestamps; no separate field needed.</li>\n</ol>\n<h3>3.3 Multi-message batch — concatenate repetitions</h3>\n<p>For <code>batch.len() == N</code> arrival events, the consumer emits the per-arrival template N times back-to-back. <strong>No outer wrapper, no banner, no instruction string, no <code>&lt;message index=N&gt;</code> tags.</strong> The next <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> opening is itself the boundary marker.</p>\n<p><strong>Example.</strong> Two messages from alice:</p>\n<ul>\n<li>M1 = &quot;look at this&quot; + screenshot</li>\n<li>M2 = audio transcript + &quot;listen to this&quot;</li>\n</ul>\n<pre><code>Vec&lt;ContentBlock&gt;:\n  Text  { &quot;&lt;sender_context&gt;\\n{...alice's JSON, timestamp=T1...}\\n&lt;/sender_context&gt;&quot; }   ← delimiter for M1\n  Text  { &quot;look at this&quot; }                                ← M1 prompt\n  Image { screenshot }                                    ← M1 attachment\n  Text  { &quot;&lt;sender_context&gt;\\n{...alice's JSON, timestamp=T2...}\\n&lt;/sender_context&gt;&quot; }   ← delimiter for M2\n  Text  { transcript content }                            ← M2 transcript (precedes prompt)\n  Text  { &quot;listen to this&quot; }                              ← M2 prompt\n</code></pre>\n<p>Boundary rule: a block belongs to the most recent <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> delimiter preceding it; the boundary moves the moment the next <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> opens.</p>\n<p>What the agent reads when ContentBlocks are concatenated logically:</p>\n<pre><code>&lt;sender_context&gt;\n{&quot;schema&quot;:&quot;openab.sender.v1&quot;,&quot;sender_id&quot;:&quot;…&quot;,&quot;sender_name&quot;:&quot;alice&quot;,&quot;display_name&quot;:&quot;alice&quot;,&quot;channel&quot;:&quot;discord&quot;,&quot;channel_id&quot;:&quot;…&quot;,&quot;is_bot&quot;:false,&quot;timestamp&quot;:&quot;2026-04-26T18:33:19.912Z&quot;}\n&lt;/sender_context&gt;\nlook at this\n[ImageBlock — screenshot]\n&lt;sender_context&gt;\n{&quot;schema&quot;:&quot;openab.sender.v1&quot;,&quot;sender_id&quot;:&quot;…&quot;,&quot;sender_name&quot;:&quot;alice&quot;,&quot;display_name&quot;:&quot;alice&quot;,&quot;channel&quot;:&quot;discord&quot;,&quot;channel_id&quot;:&quot;…&quot;,&quot;is_bot&quot;:false,&quot;timestamp&quot;:&quot;2026-04-26T18:33:23.105Z&quot;}\n&lt;/sender_context&gt;\n[TextBlock — transcript content]\nlisten to this\n</code></pre>\n<p>Properties:</p>\n<ul>\n<li><strong>Attribution is structural via array position</strong> — attachments belong to the most recent <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> preceding them in the ContentBlock array. Mirrors Discord's per-message bubble rendering.</li>\n<li><strong>Multiple attachments per message</strong> group naturally — all of M1's transcripts, prompt, and images sit between M1's <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> and M2's <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code>. Within an arrival event the order is fixed: Text <code>extra_blocks</code> (transcripts) → <code>{prompt}</code> → non-Text <code>extra_blocks</code> (images), per §3.1.</li>\n<li><strong>No ACP protocol change.</strong> Still <code>Vec&lt;ContentBlock&gt;</code> with existing block types.</li>\n</ul>\n<h3>3.4 Three-way comparison</h3>\n<table>\n<thead>\n<tr>\n<th>Aspect</th>\n<th>Current per-message (<code>adapter.rs:156-172</code>)</th>\n<th>RFC MVP (Appendix A &quot;Packing a batch&quot;)</th>\n<th>This ADR</th>\n</tr>\n</thead>\n<tbody>\n<tr>\n<td>Sender attribution</td>\n<td><code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> JSON wrapper around prompt</td>\n<td>New <code>&lt;message index=N from=&quot;…&quot;&gt;</code> attribute (parallel schema)</td>\n<td><strong>Reuse</strong> existing <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> JSON verbatim — adds <code>timestamp</code> field only</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Per-batch wrapper</td>\n<td>n/a</td>\n<td>One combined <code>Text</code> block: banner + N <code>&lt;message&gt;</code> tags</td>\n<td>One delimiter Text block + one prompt Text block + interleaved extras per arrival; no outer wrapper</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Banner / semantic framing</td>\n<td>n/a</td>\n<td><code>[Batched: N messages…]</code> always emitted</td>\n<td><strong>None.</strong> No banner, no instruction, no metadata beyond <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code></td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Boundary marker</td>\n<td>n/a</td>\n<td><code>&lt;message index=N from=&quot;…&quot;&gt;</code> opening + <code>&lt;/message&gt;</code> close</td>\n<td>A standalone <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> ContentBlock — the next delimiter opens, the previous arrival ends</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td><code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> block</td>\n<td>Prepended into the same Text block as <code>{prompt}</code></td>\n<td>n/a (wholly different schema)</td>\n<td><strong>Standalone</strong> Text block — separate from <code>{prompt}</code> block</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Text extras (transcripts)</td>\n<td>Prepended before the combined <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;+prompt</code> block (<code>adapter.rs:158-162</code>)</td>\n<td>Flattened at end of ContentBlock array</td>\n<td>Placed after the delimiter but before the <code>{prompt}</code> block — voice content reads first</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Image extras</td>\n<td>Appended after main text (<code>adapter.rs:165-169</code>)</td>\n<td>Flattened at end of ContentBlock array</td>\n<td>Appended after the <code>{prompt}</code> block (unchanged from pre-batching)</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Attachment ↔ message link</td>\n<td>Implicit (single message)</td>\n<td><strong>Lost</strong> — flattened blocks have no tie back to a sub-message (T1.4 / B1 blocker)</td>\n<td><strong>Structural by adjacency</strong> to the most recent <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> delimiter</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td><code>batch.len() == 1</code> vs <code>≥ 2</code> code paths</td>\n<td>Baseline (only path)</td>\n<td>Two paths (with/without banner-Text combination)</td>\n<td><strong>Single uniform path</strong> — N=1 is just one repetition of the same template</td>\n</tr>\n</tbody>\n</table>\n<h3>3.5 Single uniform code path</h3>\n<p>The packing is one template emitted N times — no special-case fast path for isolated messages. For <code>batch.len() == 1</code> the output is one delimiter + transcripts + prompt + images sequence, structurally equivalent to today's per-message dispatch with three small differences:</p>\n<ol>\n<li><code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> JSON now carries a <code>timestamp</code> field (additive schema change).</li>\n<li><code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> is its own ContentBlock instead of being prepended into the same Text block as <code>{prompt}</code>.</li>\n<li>STT transcripts move from <strong>before the <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> envelope</strong> (today's <code>adapter.rs:158-162</code>) to <strong>after the delimiter but before <code>{prompt}</code></strong> — image ordering (after <code>{prompt}</code>) is unchanged.</li>\n</ol>\n<p>Concretely (Scenario D below): in the current per-message path (<code>adapter.rs:158-162</code>), the transcript is prepended before the entire per-arrival template — including <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> itself — so it reads as if it were user-typed text:</p>\n<pre><code>[Voice message transcript]: hey can we sync about the deploy\n&lt;sender_context&gt;\n{&quot;schema&quot;:&quot;openab.sender.v1&quot;, ...}\n&lt;/sender_context&gt;\n\n</code></pre>\n<p>Under this ADR the transcript moves to inside the arrival event (after the delimiter, before <code>{prompt}</code>), owned by its arrival event like any other attachment. The boundary rule stays clean: <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> always opens an arrival event; transcripts/prompt/images always follow within the same arrival.</p>\n<h3>3.6 Scope of attribution — Scenarios A–D</h3>\n<p>The packing preserves <strong>structural</strong> attribution (which attachment was uploaded as part of which arrival event). It deliberately does <strong>not</strong> attempt <strong>semantic</strong> attribution (which text refers to which attachment across separate arrival events) — that is exactly the inference that should be left to the ACP agent.</p>\n<p>(Sender-context JSON is abbreviated as <code>{alice, ts=T1}</code> etc. for readability — in the real ContentBlock stream it's the full JSON record.)</p>\n<p><strong>Scenario A — text and image in the same chat message</strong> (e.g. drag-and-drop with caption)</p>\n<pre><code>&lt;sender_context&gt;{alice, ts=T1}&lt;/sender_context&gt;\nlook at this\n[ImageBlock]\n</code></pre>\n<p>The image follows alice's <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> with no other <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> between → belongs to alice's M1.</p>\n<p><strong>Scenario B — text in one message, image in the next, same author</strong> (very common: type the description, then paste the image)</p>\n<ul>\n<li>M1 (alice): &quot;see this image&quot;</li>\n<li>M2 (alice): [image, no text]</li>\n</ul>\n<pre><code>&lt;sender_context&gt;{alice, ts=T1}&lt;/sender_context&gt;\nsee this image\n&lt;sender_context&gt;{alice, ts=T2}&lt;/sender_context&gt;\n[ImageBlock]\n</code></pre>\n<p>M2 has no <code>{prompt}</code> block (empty prompt is omitted, §3.1). Broker keeps the structural truth (image arrived as M2, alone). The agent reads identical <code>sender_id</code> on both <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> blocks and trivially infers M1's &quot;this image&quot; refers to M2's attachment. The <code>timestamp</code> delta <code>T2 − T1</code> reinforces this when M1 and M2 are seconds apart.</p>\n<p><strong>Scenario C — fragmented multi-author batch</strong> (alice's text → bob's interjection → alice's image)</p>\n<ul>\n<li>M1 (alice): &quot;see this image&quot;</li>\n<li>M2 (bob): &quot;what?&quot;</li>\n<li>M3 (alice): [image, no text]</li>\n</ul>\n<pre><code>&lt;sender_context&gt;{alice, sender_id=A, ts=T1}&lt;/sender_context&gt;\nsee this image\n&lt;sender_context&gt;{bob, sender_id=B, ts=T2}&lt;/sender_context&gt;\nwhat?\n&lt;sender_context&gt;{alice, sender_id=A, ts=T3}&lt;/sender_context&gt;\n[ImageBlock]\n</code></pre>\n<p>The broker does not &quot;skip&quot; bob's message or re-link alice's M1 ↔ M3 — those are semantic decisions. The repeated <code>sender_id=A</code> lets the agent group by stable user ID across non-adjacent messages; bob's interjection is preserved as-is so the agent can decide whether to address it.</p>\n<p><strong>Scenario D — voice-only message in a batch (existing STT path)</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li>M1 (alice): &quot;look at this&quot; + screenshot</li>\n<li>M2 (alice): voice-only — <code>msg.content</code> empty; <code>discord.rs:524</code> produces a <code>[Voice message transcript]: …</code> Text block in <code>extra_blocks</code></li>\n<li>M3 (bob): &quot;what?&quot;</li>\n</ul>\n<pre><code>&lt;sender_context&gt;{alice, ts=T1}&lt;/sender_context&gt;\nlook at this\n[ImageBlock]\n&lt;sender_context&gt;{alice, ts=T2}&lt;/sender_context&gt;\n[Voice message transcript]: hey can we sync about the deploy\n&lt;sender_context&gt;{bob, ts=T3}&lt;/sender_context&gt;\nwhat?\n</code></pre>\n<p>M2 has empty <code>{prompt}</code> (so the prompt block is omitted, §3.1) and one transcript block. The transcript lands immediately after the delimiter — within M2's arrival, before any <code>{prompt}</code> block would appear.</p>\n<p><strong>Behavior change vs. v0.8.2-beta.1:</strong> in the per-message path (<code>adapter.rs:158-162</code>) the transcript is <em>prepended</em> before <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> so it reads as if it were the user's typed text. Under this ADR the transcript moves to <em>inside the arrival event</em>, after the <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> delimiter and before <code>{prompt}</code>, owned by M2 like any other attachment. The agent still sees the transcript content — just one block down, with the sender envelope explicitly framing it.</p>\n<p><strong>Rollback path if cross-agent smoke fails.</strong> If a Phase 1 cross-agent smoke fixture (Scenario D against Claude Code, Cursor, and Copilot) shows any target regressing on voice-only handling, the response is a code change, not a runtime toggle. The hotfix restores the v0.8.2-beta.1 single-message voice layout in two steps inside <code>pack_arrival_event</code>: (1) re-introduce the <code>extra_blocks.len() == 1 &amp;&amp; prompt.is_empty()</code> special case that treats the transcript as a <code>{prompt}</code> substitute; (2) for that case, fold <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> back into the same Text block as the substituted prompt (the combined-block layout). Both steps are needed — the standalone-delimiter split (§3 change 2) and the transcript-position move (§3 change 3) are independent and either alone could surface the regression. <strong>No always-on feature flag.</strong> The cross-agent smoke fixture is the gate; a hotfix PR is the rollback mechanism.</p>\n<p>The principle (instance of I3): <strong>structural truth is non-negotiable, semantic interpretation is deferred.</strong></p>\n<h3>3.7 Inbound Discord field fidelity (scope clarification)</h3>\n<p>Today's broker (<code>discord.rs:480-483</code>) extracts only <code>msg.content</code> and <code>msg.attachments</code> from inbound Discord messages. Other fields — <code>embeds[]</code> (including auto-generated link previews), <code>stickers</code>, <code>reactions</code>, <code>reference</code> (reply chain) — are silently dropped. Dispatched ContentBlocks reflect only the fields openab currently ingests; <strong>I3 applies to those fields specifically</strong>. Closing the inbound-fidelity gap is tracked as a follow-up and is out of scope for this ADR.</p>\n<hr />\n<h2>4. Configuration &amp; Rollout</h2>\n<h3>4.1 Config schema</h3>\n<pre><code class=\"language-toml\">[discord]\nmessage_processing_mode = &quot;per-message&quot;  # default in Phase 1\n# Or:\nmessage_processing_mode = &quot;per-thread&quot;   # one buffer per (platform, thread)\n# Or:\nmessage_processing_mode = &quot;per-lane&quot;     # one buffer per (platform, thread, sender)\nmax_buffered_messages   = 10             # per-thread / per-lane only; mpsc cap\nmax_batch_tokens        = 24000          # per-thread / per-lane only; soft cap on cumulative tokens\n\n# Slack and Gateway adapters expose the same three keys under [slack] / [gateway].\n</code></pre>\n<p><code>message_processing_mode</code> is <strong>3-valued</strong> (<code>per-message</code> / <code>per-thread</code> / <code>per-lane</code>). All three flow through the same <code>Dispatcher::submit</code> path; they differ only in how the dispatcher derives the mpsc identity (<code>Dispatcher::key</code>) and what consumer idle timeout it uses (§6.10):</p>\n<table>\n<thead>\n<tr>\n<th>Mode</th>\n<th>mpsc cap</th>\n<th>dispatcher key</th>\n<th>Idle timeout</th>\n<th>When to pick</th>\n</tr>\n</thead>\n<tbody>\n<tr>\n<td><code>per-message</code></td>\n<td><strong>1</strong></td>\n<td><code>(platform, thread_id)</code></td>\n<td>10s (<code>PER_MESSAGE_CONSUMER_IDLE_TIMEOUT</code>)</td>\n<td>Default in Phase 1 — preserves v0.8.2-beta.1 dispatch shape (each message dispatches alone, FIFO via the dispatcher), with the structural changes from §3 (split <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> block, transcript ordering).</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td><code>per-thread</code></td>\n<td>configured</td>\n<td><code>(platform, thread_id)</code></td>\n<td>300s (<code>DEFAULT_CONSUMER_IDLE_TIMEOUT</code>)</td>\n<td>One buffer per thread regardless of sender — turn-boundary batching as originally designed. Multiple senders in the same thread share a buffer and produce one ACP turn covering all of them.</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td><code>per-lane</code></td>\n<td>configured</td>\n<td><code>(platform, thread_id, sender_id)</code></td>\n<td>300s (<code>DEFAULT_CONSUMER_IDLE_TIMEOUT</code>)</td>\n<td>One buffer per (thread × sender) — appropriate when peer bots and humans share a thread but their inputs should batch independently. Each sender gets their own mpsc + consumer; all senders still serialize through the shared <code>Arc&lt;Mutex&lt;AcpConnection&gt;&gt;</code> per thread.</td>\n</tr>\n</tbody>\n</table>\n<p><strong>Session pool keying is unchanged across all three modes</strong> — the ACP session is per-thread (<code>(platform, thread_id)</code>); only the dispatcher's mpsc identity varies. In <code>per-lane</code> mode the per-lane consumers compete for the same connection mutex; per-thread sequential ACP-turn order is preserved by the mutex, while per-lane FIFO order is preserved by each lane's mpsc.</p>\n<p><strong>Why <code>per-message</code> still uses the dispatcher (cap=1)</strong> instead of bypassing it: keeping a uniform code path means <code>cancel_buffered_thread</code>, sweep, <code>SendError</code> recovery (§2.5), and observability (§6.6) work identically across modes — there is no &quot;per-message has its own dispatch path&quot; to maintain. The cap=1 buffer adds μs-scale handle lookup; ACP turn duration dominates by 4–6 orders of magnitude.</p>\n<p><strong>Legacy <code>&quot;batched&quot;</code> alias is rejected</strong> — earlier drafts of this ADR used a 2-valued mode (<code>per-message</code> / <code>batched</code>); configs still using <code>&quot;batched&quot;</code> must migrate to either <code>per-thread</code> or <code>per-lane</code> explicitly. The deserializer rejects unknown values with a clear error so silent fallthrough cannot happen.</p>\n<h3>4.2 Sizing <code>max_buffered_messages</code></h3>\n<p>The default of 10 covers human-only fragmentation comfortably (typical human typing rate caps at ~3 messages per 30s). For <strong>multi-bot collaboration</strong> channels, however, peer bots can push burst rates well past that. Sampling three multi-bot threads in an early opt-in deployment (~300–1000 messages each, accumulated over several days):</p>\n<table>\n<thead>\n<tr>\n<th>Thread</th>\n<th>Human msgs (max in 30s / 60s)</th>\n<th>Peer-bot msgs (max in 30s / 60s)</th>\n<th>All incoming (max in 30s / 60s)</th>\n</tr>\n</thead>\n<tbody>\n<tr>\n<td>Active project thread (~1000 msgs)</td>\n<td>3 / 3</td>\n<td>12 / 16</td>\n<td>12 / 16</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Status report thread (~360 msgs)</td>\n<td>2 / 3</td>\n<td>11 / 20</td>\n<td>11 / 20</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Task triage thread (~300 msgs)</td>\n<td>2 / 2</td>\n<td>24 / 24</td>\n<td>24 / 24</td>\n</tr>\n</tbody>\n</table>\n<p>Humans alone never exceeded 3 messages in 30s; peer bots drove all of the burstiness. After this sampling the deployment raised the cap to <strong>30</strong> (~25% headroom over the largest observed 60s burst).</p>\n<p>Guidance: human-only adapters use 10; multi-bot adapters size to observed peer-bot burst rate with headroom (typically 20–50). <strong>Backpressure ≠ data loss</strong> — when full, <code>submit</code> parks the calling task per-thread; nothing is dropped. Undersizing only produces &quot;more, smaller batches&quot;, not lost messages — start at the default and tune up after observing real burst patterns in <code>dispatch</code> debug logs.</p>\n<h3>4.3 Sizing <code>max_batch_tokens</code></h3>\n<p>Default <strong>24000</strong>, sized below typical ACP CLI context budgets with headroom for system prompt + accumulated history. The greedy drain stops when either the count cap or the token cap fires; remaining messages stay in the channel for the next turn (FIFO preserved).</p>\n<ul>\n<li><code>BufferedMessage.estimated_tokens</code> is computed at enqueue from prompt text + extra_blocks; image blocks use a coarse fixed estimate.</li>\n<li>Token estimation is intentionally rough — the goal is a guard rail, not an exact pre-flight. Under-estimating splits a batch that could have fit; over-estimating splits one extra time. Both are recoverable.</li>\n<li><strong>Splitting only at message boundaries</strong> — never inside a single arrival event. A single oversized message dispatches alone (broker does not split, truncate, or summarize a single arrival event to fit; cf. §6.4 rule 7); the ACP CLI's own context-overflow error surfaces normally.</li>\n</ul>\n<h3>4.4 Phases</h3>\n<pre><code>Phase 1 — Mechanism + T1 dispositions (single PR, Discord + Slack + Gateway)\n  - New module: src/dispatch.rs (Dispatcher + ThreadHandle + consumer_loop)\n  - pack_arrival_event lives on adapter.rs (single packing path for all modes, §3)\n  - 3-valued MessageProcessingMode enum in config (Message / Thread / Lane;\n    default = Message)\n  - All three modes go through Dispatcher::submit; mode controls\n    (cap, BatchGrouping, idle_timeout):\n      Message -&gt; (1, BatchGrouping::Thread, PER_MESSAGE_CONSUMER_IDLE_TIMEOUT)\n      Thread  -&gt; (max_buffered_messages, BatchGrouping::Thread, DEFAULT_CONSUMER_IDLE_TIMEOUT)\n      Lane    -&gt; (max_buffered_messages, BatchGrouping::Lane,   DEFAULT_CONSUMER_IDLE_TIMEOUT)\n  - Discord wiring (discord.rs:600-608): unconditional dispatcher.submit()\n  - Slack wiring: platform preprocessing moved before dispatcher.submit();\n    KeyedAsyncQueue removed — Dispatcher consumer task takes over per-thread serialization\n  - Gateway wiring: router.handle_message() replaced with dispatcher.submit()\n  - Packing (§3): SenderContext.timestamp additive; pack_arrival_event uniform\n    across modes; &lt;sender_context&gt; emitted as standalone Text block (delimiter);\n    transcripts placed between delimiter and {prompt}; images placed after {prompt}\n  - SendError handling (§2.5): proactive is_finished cleanup + transparent retry\n    once; ❌ + ⚠️ + return Err only if the retry also fails\n  - submit does NOT touch last_active (§2.7)\n  - other_bot_present bool snapshot on BufferedMessage; consumer reads batch.last() at dispatch (§2.6)\n  - Dispatcher::per_thread uses std::sync::Mutex; ThreadHandle.generation: u64\n  - sweep_stale: periodic eviction of consumers idle longer than idle_timeout\n    (one-shot threads never trigger lazy eviction by themselves; sweep keeps\n    HashMap bounded — see §6.10)\n  - max_buffered_messages configurable (default 10, multi-bot 30) — per-thread / per-lane only\n  - max_batch_tokens soft cap on greedy drain (default 24000) — per-thread / per-lane only\n  - Reactions: queued (👀) reaction on ALL messages in batch before dispatch (§6.7);\n    applied sequentially (not parallel) to preserve message-ID order in the\n    Discord/Slack reaction list; trailing message anchors StatusReactionController progress\n  - /cancel-all command + Dispatcher::cancel_buffered_thread (uses generation field)\n  - Tracing spans: buffer_wait_ms / agent_dispatch_ms / batch_size (§6.5)\n  - SIGTERM: log per-thread buffered count before drop (§6.6)\n  - Cross-agent recognition smoke fixture (Claude Code / Cursor / Copilot — Scenario D)\n  - SendError manual staging smoke entry (§6.11)\n\n  Tests:\n    - per-message mode: single-message dispatch, structurally equivalent to v0.8.2-beta.1\n      modulo §3 split-block layout\n    - per-thread mode: 3-message fragmentation merges into one batch\n    - per-thread mode: new message arrives mid-turn, joins next batch\n    - per-lane mode: two senders in same thread → two independent buffers, two\n      consumers, but serialized through shared connection mutex\n    - per-lane mode: dispatcher key shape is {platform}:{thread}:{sender}\n    - /cancel during a batched turn does not drop buffer\n    - /cancel-all drops buffered messages and aborts consumer\n    - SendError → proactive is_finished cleanup + transparent retry; happy\n      path emits no user-visible signal; failing-retry path: ❌ + ⚠️ + Err\n    - concurrent SendError → only one eviction; both observers reach the\n      retry path on their own consumers\n    - buffer-full → submit parks (no Err, no reaction, no ⚠️)\n    - other_bot_present freshness (3-turn timeline)\n    - oversized batch (cumulative tokens &gt; cap) splits across two ACP turns; FIFO preserved\n    - single message &gt; max_batch_tokens dispatches alone; ACP error surfaces normally\n    - voice-only Scenario D pack output\n    - queued reaction applied to all batch messages before dispatch (sequential)\n    - Scenario B packing: image in separate message from text (same author) — structural adjacency preserved\n    - Scenario C packing: multi-author interleaved batch — per-sender attribution preserved across non-adjacent messages\n    - per-mode idle timeout: PerMessage consumer evicts after 10s idle; per-thread/per-lane after 300s\n\nPhase 2 — Validation\n  - Roll out to a single channel (e.g. dev sandbox)\n  - Compare turn counts, latency distributions, user-reported quality\n  - Multi-chunk output fan-out under larger batched payloads (split_message line-boundary\n    edge cases, placeholder-edit-before-followup ordering, Discord rate-limit headroom,\n    chunks_per_response distribution)\n  - Per-channel config override ([discord.channels.&lt;id&gt;] for max_buffered_messages,\n    message_processing_mode)\n  - Gateway per-platform batching validation\n  - Per-thread vs per-lane comparison on multi-bot threads (which mode produces\n    cleaner ACP output for peer-bot interleaving)\n\nPhase 3 — Default flip (separate RFC if needed)\n  - Promote per-thread or per-lane to default (decision deferred to Phase 2 data)\n  - Or: keep per-message default if Phase 2 shows no real-world batching wins\n</code></pre>\n<h3>4.5 Adapter integration pattern</h3>\n<p>All adapters follow a canonical structure:</p>\n<pre><code>Platform event loop  (single async task, naturally serial)\n  ↓\n[Before spawn — serial, in event loop]\n  bot_turns / gating checks\n  ↓\ntokio::spawn {\n    // 1. Platform-specific preprocessing (parallel across messages, no shared state)\n    resolve_user_id() / file download / STT / extra_blocks assembly\n    ↓\n    // 2. Uniform handoff — platform-agnostic from here\n    dispatcher.submit(thread_key, BufferedMessage, ...)\n      └─ tx.send() → returns immediately\n}\n\n─── consumer_loop (one per active thread) ───\nrx.recv() → greedy drain → dispatch_batch()\n  ↓\npack_arrival_event() × N → Vec&lt;ContentBlock&gt;\n  ↓\npool.with_connection() → conn.lock() → session_prompt()\n</code></pre>\n<p><code>Dispatcher</code> is fully platform-agnostic — it only sees <code>BufferedMessage</code>, never raw platform events. Platform-specific preprocessing runs in parallel across concurrent messages (no shared mutable state). <code>bot_turns</code> and gating checks remain before spawn, in the serial event loop. Future adapters (Telegram, Teams, LINE, etc.) should follow this pattern from the start; <code>KeyedAsyncQueue</code> should not be introduced in new adapters.</p>\n<h3>4.6 Migration path</h3>\n<p>LINE-style atomic cut-over is not required. In Phase 1 <code>message_processing_mode</code> is a per-adapter config flag (<code>[discord]</code> / <code>[slack]</code> / <code>[gateway]</code>) that operators flip without external coordination; per-channel override (<code>[discord.channels.&lt;id&gt;].message_processing_mode</code>) lands in Phase 2 (§4.4). The conservative Phase 1 default (<code>per-message</code>) keeps the rollout safe; flipping the default is left to Phase 3 after a validation period.</p>\n<hr />\n<h2>5. Alternatives Considered</h2>\n<h3>5.1 Mechanism alternatives</h3>\n<p><strong>Per-message dispatch (status quo, v0.8.2-beta.1).</strong> The baseline. Each arrival becomes its own ACP turn. <strong>Rejected as the steady state</strong> because turns 1..N-1 may waste work (intermediate output, redundant tool invocations) before turn N arrives with the corrected intent — which is exactly the workload §1.1 documents. Retained as the Phase 1 default and as the per-message mode of the adapter config flag for safe rollback.</p>\n<p><strong>Pre-turn debouncing.</strong> Wait <code>debounce_ms</code> after each message before dispatching (e.g. Hermes' adapter-level <code>_pending_text_batches</code>, ~0.6–2.0s). <strong>Rejected</strong> because it imposes a latency floor on every message including isolated ones, violating I1. The buffering-during-turn approach pays zero added latency for isolated messages because the turn duration itself is the natural buffering window, used for free.</p>\n<p><strong>Single-slot in-flight overwrite (Hermes pattern).</strong> When a new message arrives during an in-flight turn, overwrite the previous pending message and signal an interrupt to the agent loop. <strong>Rejected on two counts.</strong> First, it drops messages: M2 is overwritten by M3 on rapid-fire bursts, with no recovery. Second, it requires mid-turn interrupt of the agent — possible for Hermes / OpenClaw because their agent loop is in-process (asyncio), but <strong>not possible for openab</strong> because the agent is an external ACP CLI (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex) that yields control only at turn end. This is an architectural constraint, not a design choice.</p>\n<p><strong>Mid-turn interrupt.</strong> Cancel the in-flight ACP turn when a new message arrives, restart with combined context. <strong>Rejected — same architectural constraint as above.</strong> External ACP CLIs do not expose an interrupt protocol that yields control between tool calls; <code>/cancel</code> aborts at turn boundary, not mid-stream.</p>\n<p><strong>Topic detection / semantic grouping in broker.</strong> Apply rules (&quot;same user + &lt; 3s gap = merge&quot;) or an LLM classifier to decide which messages to merge into one ACP turn. <strong>Rejected — violates I3.</strong> Real grouping is <em>semantic</em> (was message N+1 a continuation of N's intent, an unrelated topic, a correction?); the broker has no way to answer that without an LLM, and the user's ACP session <strong>already has</strong> the full context and is the right place to make semantic decisions.</p>\n<p><strong>Per-channel or global buffer keying.</strong> Aggregate messages across threads in a channel (or globally across channels). <strong>Rejected</strong> because conversation scope in openab = thread; per-thread keying matches the existing <code>Arc&lt;Mutex&lt;AcpConnection&gt;&gt;</code> keying. Cross-thread merging would conflate independent conversations.</p>\n<p><strong>HTTP-style request coalescing in the per-connection mutex itself.</strong> Retrofit batching onto the Tokio Mutex's waker list. <strong>Rejected</strong> because Tokio Mutex wakers are opaque: the mutex sees only &quot;someone is waiting&quot; and cannot enumerate pending messages, inspect content, or batch them. Batching requires an explicit queue at a layer that owns the message data — that's the dispatcher.</p>\n<h3>5.2 Packing alternatives</h3>\n<p><strong>RFC MVP wrapper-and-flatten</strong> — wrap each sub-message text in <code>&lt;message index=N from=&quot;…&quot;&gt;…&lt;/message&gt;</code> and flatten all sub-messages' <code>extra_blocks</code> into a single tail of the ContentBlock array. <strong>Rejected</strong> for two failures: (1) attribution loss (T1.4 / B1) — image and transcript blocks at the tail have no tie back to a <code>&lt;message index=N&gt;</code>, so the agent can't know which image belongs to which sub-message; (2) parallel sender-encoding schemes — <code>from=&quot;alice&quot;</code> duplicates information already in <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> JSON's <code>display_name</code> and risks drift if one schema evolves and the other doesn't.</p>\n<p><strong>RFC MVP wrapper, <code>extra_blocks</code> placed inside the <code>&lt;message&gt;</code> tag.</strong> A patch on the above: place each sub-message's <code>extra_blocks</code> immediately after its <code>&lt;message index=N&gt;</code> tag (JARVIS's suggested fix). <strong>Rejected</strong> because the same fix is achievable using <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> itself as the boundary marker — no need to introduce a parallel <code>&lt;message&gt;</code> schema. §3's design is the same fix expressed without the new wrapper tag.</p>\n<p><strong>Keep current asymmetric ordering as a special case.</strong> Preserve <code>adapter.rs:158-169</code> ordering via an <code>extra_blocks.len() == 1 &amp;&amp; prompt.is_empty()</code> branch on every single-message dispatch. <strong>Rejected.</strong> Single uniform code path beats a fast-path branch for a marginal Scenario D readability difference. Scenario D's behavior change is reversible if cross-agent smoke shows real disruption (§3.6 rollback).</p>\n<p><strong>Inject a leading <code>[Batched: N messages…]</code> banner string.</strong> <strong>Rejected — violates I3.</strong> Broker injecting framing is a semantic directive (&quot;treat these as one logical unit&quot;) that the agent can no longer un-see. Whether to treat the messages as one logical unit is the kind of judgment the agent should make from the structural facts (same <code>sender_id</code>, close <code>timestamp</code> deltas), not from a broker hint.</p>\n<p><strong>Sidecar metadata block (JSON map).</strong> Single trailing JSON block describing per-arrival attribution — e.g. <code>{&quot;events&quot;:[{&quot;index&quot;:0,&quot;sender_id&quot;:&quot;A&quot;,&quot;ts&quot;:&quot;…&quot;,&quot;attachment_indices&quot;:[2,3]}, …]}</code> — appended once at the end of the ContentBlock array, with all <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> headers removed and prompts concatenated. <strong>Rejected</strong> for three reasons: (1) single-sequence readability — pushing attribution into a tail JSON forces the agent to cross-reference <code>attachment_indices</code> against array positions, losing the affordance that adjacency provides for free; (2) parser coupling — introduces a second schema, duplicating the failure mode of the parallel <code>&lt;message&gt;</code> tag; (3) ACP / tool-use mismatch risk — some agents may treat trailing JSON as a tool-result fragment or post-prompt instruction.</p>\n<h3>5.3 Prior art</h3>\n<p>Two adjacent systems solve &quot;user typed multiple times in quick succession&quot; with different trade-offs. Both are personal AI agent runtimes (single-user, agent loop bundled into the gateway process) — different shape from openab's multi-tenant broker, but the in-flight buffering problem is the same.</p>\n<table>\n<thead>\n<tr>\n<th>Aspect</th>\n<th>Hermes Agent</th>\n<th>OpenClaw</th>\n<th>Current openab</th>\n<th>This ADR</th>\n</tr>\n</thead>\n<tbody>\n<tr>\n<td>Shape</td>\n<td>Single-user runtime, gateway = agent</td>\n<td>Single-user runtime</td>\n<td>Multi-tenant broker → external ACP CLI</td>\n<td>Same as current</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>First-message latency</td>\n<td>~0.6–2.0s (Discord adapter debounce — API split compensation, not user-intent batching)</td>\n<td>n/a observed</td>\n<td><strong>0</strong> (immediate dispatch)</td>\n<td><strong>0</strong> (preserved)</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Adapter-level batching</td>\n<td><code>_pending_text_batches</code>, <code>_text_batch_split_delay_seconds</code> — reassembles &gt;2000-char Discord-auto-chunked messages</td>\n<td><code>extensions/discord/src/monitor/message-handler.ts</code> (preflight debounce only — not in-flight turn-boundary batching)</td>\n<td>None</td>\n<td>None (deliberate)</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>In-flight new message</td>\n<td>Single-slot <code>_pending_messages[key]</code> — <strong>overwrites prior</strong> + <code>interrupt_event.set()</code> cancels in-flight</td>\n<td>n/a observed</td>\n<td>N independent <code>tokio::spawn</code> tasks each park on per-thread mutex</td>\n<td>Send to per-thread bounded <code>mpsc</code>; consumer batches at turn boundary</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Buffer data structure</td>\n<td><code>Dict[str, MessageEvent]</code> (1 slot)</td>\n<td>—</td>\n<td>None (mutex waker list, opaque)</td>\n<td>bounded <code>mpsc::channel</code> (FIFO, default cap 10)</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>3 fast messages → ACP turns</td>\n<td><strong>1 turn</strong>, middle message dropped by overwrite</td>\n<td>—</td>\n<td><strong>3 turns</strong>, intermediate output wasted</td>\n<td><strong>2 turns</strong> (M1, then batch [M2, M3]) — no message lost</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Mid-turn interrupt</td>\n<td><strong>Yes</strong> (asyncio interrupt event) — agent loop is in-process</td>\n<td>—</td>\n<td>No</td>\n<td>No</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Same-thread message ordering</td>\n<td>(1-slot makes this moot)</td>\n<td>—</td>\n<td>Approximate (Tokio Mutex not strictly FIFO)</td>\n<td>Strict (mpsc FIFO)</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Per-key serialization</td>\n<td><code>asyncio.Event</code> + <code>_active_sessions</code> dict</td>\n<td><code>src/plugin-sdk/keyed-async-queue.ts</code></td>\n<td><code>KeyedAsyncQueue</code> (per-key Semaphore, Slack) + <code>Arc&lt;Mutex&lt;AcpConnection&gt;&gt;</code></td>\n<td>Inherited</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Bot-message gating</td>\n<td><code>DISCORD_ALLOW_BOTS</code> (off / mentions / all)</td>\n<td>n/a observed</td>\n<td><code>allow_bot_messages</code> (3-value, borrowed from Hermes)</td>\n<td>Inherited</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Stall UX feedback</td>\n<td>—</td>\n<td><code>extensions/discord/src/monitor/inbound-worker.ts</code></td>\n<td><code>reactions.rs</code> stall_soft / stall_hard (borrowed from OpenClaw)</td>\n<td>Inherited</td>\n</tr>\n</tbody>\n</table>\n<p><strong>Three trade-off axes:</strong></p>\n<ol>\n<li><strong>Drop vs preserve.</strong> Hermes' single-slot overwrite drops middle messages in fast bursts; openab (current and ADR) preserves all.</li>\n<li><strong>Interrupt vs wait for boundary.</strong> Hermes can interrupt the in-flight LLM call because the agent loop is in-process. openab cannot — the agent is an external ACP CLI that yields control only at turn end. This is an <em>architectural</em> constraint, not a design choice. The ADR turns it into a feature: the existing turn duration is the natural buffering window, with no added latency for isolated messages.</li>\n<li><strong>Debounce vs piggyback.</strong> Hermes' Discord adapter pays ~0.6–2.0s per message regardless (for API split compensation). The ADR pays 0 for isolated messages — buffering only fills <em>during</em> an active turn, when the user is already waiting on the agent.</li>\n</ol>\n<p><strong>Conclusion:</strong> Neither Hermes nor OpenClaw implements turn-boundary batching. This ADR's design is novel among these three systems — it turns the architectural constraint (no mid-turn interrupt for external ACP CLIs) into a feature (zero-latency first message + lossless FIFO buffering during active turns).</p>\n<p><strong>Note on OpenClaw source paths:</strong> <code>stall-watchdog.ts</code> does not exist in the current OpenClaw repo — stall handling lives in <code>extensions/discord/src/monitor/inbound-worker.ts</code>.</p>\n<p>HTTP request coalescing in proxies (Varnish, nginx) — same shape (&quot;while one request is in flight, batch / dedupe others&quot;) in a different domain.</p>\n<hr />\n<h2>6. Consequences &amp; Compliance</h2>\n<h3>6.1 Positive</h3>\n<ul>\n<li><strong>First-message latency unchanged at zero</strong> — I1 preserved in steady state.</li>\n<li><strong>Wasted intermediate output eliminated</strong> for fragmented input — turn 1's full output + tool execution before turn 3 supersedes it never gets generated. Saved tokens scale with input fragmentation.</li>\n<li><strong>Deterministic same-thread ordering</strong> — strict FIFO via per-thread <code>mpsc::channel</code> replaces the not-strictly-FIFO Tokio Mutex waker list.</li>\n<li><strong>Attachment attribution recoverable by adjacency</strong> (§3) — closes T1.4 / B1 with one structural change.</li>\n<li><strong>No new packing schema invented.</strong> Reuses <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> (already known to every ACP agent that consumes today's per-message format) plus one additive <code>timestamp</code> field. <code>schema</code> stays <code>openab.sender.v1</code>.</li>\n<li><strong>Subsumes T2.b</strong> (<code>sender_name</code> disambiguation) — <code>sender_id</code> is already in <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> JSON.</li>\n<li><strong>Subsumes T2.j</strong> (<code>arrived_at_relative</code> offset) — agent computes any relative offset from absolute <code>timestamp</code>s.</li>\n<li><strong>Single uniform packing code path.</strong> N=1 and N≥2 share the exact same packer.</li>\n<li><strong>No ACP protocol change.</strong> Still <code>Vec&lt;ContentBlock&gt;</code> with existing block types.</li>\n<li><strong>Validated end-to-end on a staging deployment</strong> (2026-04-27, k9). Per-arrival shape and <code>timestamp</code> field confirmed under organic traffic; multi-message batch concatenation (<code>batch_size=2</code>) confirmed to produce a single streaming-edit reply per batch.</li>\n</ul>\n<h3>6.2 Negative</h3>\n<ul>\n<li><strong>Multi-message batches lower the ACP-turn count visible to ops.</strong> <code>bot_turns</code> ingest counter (<code>slack.rs:672-696</code>) runs before the dispatcher, so per-message loop limits still fire correctly. The downstream &quot;ACP turns&quot; metric shifts to count batches; document it.</li>\n<li><strong><code>/cancel</code> cancels one ACP turn that may now contain multiple user messages.</strong> Documented: &quot;cancel current ACP work; buffered messages fire next.&quot; <code>/cancel-all</code> covers drop-on-cancel (Phase 1).</li>\n<li><strong>§2.7 zombie blast radius widens under batching</strong> until the dedicated follow-up lands. Phase 1 is no-worse-than-released (it does not amplify the bug, but does not fix the underlying <code>cleanup_idle.try_lock</code> skip either).</li>\n<li><strong>Scenario D regression even in <code>per-message</code> mode.</strong> STT voice transcripts move from prepended-before-<code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> to placed-between-delimiter-and-prompt, changing the read order for single-message voice dispatches. The change is structural (it affects all three modes — <code>per-message</code> included — because all share the §3 packing path). Reversible via a special case if cross-agent smoke shows real disruption.</li>\n<li><strong><code>{prompt}</code> empty case is structurally valid.</strong> Voice-only / attachment-only messages produce an empty line between <code>&lt;/sender_context&gt;</code> and the first attachment block. Agents that strictly validate &quot;non-empty prompt&quot; need to relax that assumption — but this is already the case for any voice-only message under today's format.</li>\n<li><strong>Cross-agent recognition risk.</strong> Multi-<code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> repetition is a new shape from the agent's perspective. Existing single-<code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> parsing should generalize naturally (it's just the same envelope opening twice), but Phase 1 includes a manual cross-agent smoke fixture against Claude Code, Cursor, and Copilot.</li>\n<li><strong>Token-cost surface widens.</strong> Each repetition re-emits the full <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> JSON. For multi-bot channels with <code>max_buffered_messages = 30</code>, the per-batch envelope overhead is non-trivial. <code>max_batch_tokens</code> (default 24000) bounds total batch size — drain stops when either count or token cap fires, splitting only at message boundaries.</li>\n</ul>\n<h3>6.3 Neutral</h3>\n<ul>\n<li><strong><code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> proliferation in agent-visible context.</strong> The agent now sees N <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> blocks per batched turn instead of one. This is the intended structural fact, not noise — agents that previously parsed exactly one block per turn need to handle the N≥2 case, but the parsing rule is the same.</li>\n<li><strong><code>timestamp</code> is wall-clock visible.</strong> Discord/Slack already display the same timestamps to all participants in the channel; this is not a new exposure.</li>\n<li><strong>Behavior change observable to every user of an adapter once batched modes are enabled.</strong> Mitigated by <code>per-message</code> being the Phase 1 default; <code>per-thread</code> / <code>per-lane</code> are explicitly opted into per adapter, and a default flip is deferred to Phase 3 after validation.</li>\n</ul>\n<h3>6.4 Compliance rules</h3>\n<p>The rules below operationalize I3 (broker structural fidelity). Together they form the test surface that any future packing or dispatch change is judged against.</p>\n<ol>\n<li>\n<p><strong>Broker forwards <code>{prompt}</code> verbatim.</strong> Broker must not parse, classify, transform, summarize, or annotate the user-supplied text content within <code>{prompt}</code>. Any future feature that needs to inspect <code>{prompt}</code> content must do so without mutating what the agent receives.</p>\n<p><em>Note: Adapter-level preprocessing that runs before <code>{prompt}</code> is constructed (e.g. <code>resolve_mentions()</code> in <code>discord.rs</code>) is not subject to this rule. This rule applies to the broker/dispatcher layer — i.e. from <code>Dispatcher::submit</code> onward.</em></p>\n<p><strong>Counter-examples (prohibited):</strong> broker stripping markdown formatting before dispatch; broker expanding Discord <code>&lt;@123&gt;</code> mentions to <code>@username</code> strings; broker appending an <code>[image attached]</code> string when an image accompanies the prompt; broker collapsing repeated whitespace; broker normalizing Unicode forms.</p>\n</li>\n<li>\n<p><strong>No banners or framing strings.</strong> Broker must not inject any leading or trailing instruction text into the dispatched batch (e.g. no <code>[Batched: N messages…]</code>, no <code>[End of batch]</code>). All metadata lives in <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> JSON.</p>\n</li>\n<li>\n<p><strong>No wrapper tags beyond <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code>.</strong> Multi-message batches are produced by repeating the per-arrival template; no <code>&lt;message&gt;</code>, <code>&lt;batch&gt;</code>, or other wrapper schema is introduced. Future schema needs are extended as additive fields inside <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> JSON, not as new XML tags.</p>\n</li>\n<li>\n<p><strong>Attachment attribution is structural via array position.</strong> Broker must place each arrival event's <code>extra_blocks</code> between that event's <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> delimiter and the next event's <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> delimiter (i.e. inside the same arrival event), in the same order they were received from the platform adapter. Within an arrival, Text <code>extra_blocks</code> precede <code>{prompt}</code> and non-Text <code>extra_blocks</code> follow <code>{prompt}</code> (§3.1). No reordering, no deduplication, no cross-arrival re-attribution.</p>\n<p><strong>Counter-examples (prohibited):</strong> broker sorting <code>extra_blocks</code> by type (e.g. all images first, then transcripts); broker hoisting all images of a batch to a &quot;gallery&quot; section at the end; broker deduplicating two identical images sent in the same batch; broker re-attributing M2's image to M1 because M1 had text and M2 was image-only.</p>\n</li>\n<li>\n<p><strong><code>SenderContext</code> schema is additive.</strong> New fields may be added under the <code>openab.sender.v1</code> name; field removal or semantic change requires a <code>v2</code> bump and a migration path for downstream agents.</p>\n</li>\n<li>\n<p><strong><code>timestamp</code> is platform message creation time when available.</strong> Discord and Slack adapters must use the platform's own message creation timestamp. The gateway adapter's receive-time fallback must be documented as best-effort to downstream consumers.</p>\n</li>\n<li>\n<p><strong>Splitting only at message boundaries.</strong> When the token-budget cap (<code>max_batch_tokens</code>) forces a batch to split across multiple ACP turns, the split must occur between two arrival events — never inside a single arrival event. A single oversized message dispatches alone; the broker does not truncate or summarize it.</p>\n</li>\n<li>\n<p><strong>No silent failure on consumer death (retry-failed case).</strong> When <code>submit</code> observes <code>SendError</code> (consumer task death), it first attempts a transparent retry — evict the dead consumer, spawn a fresh one, and re-send (§2.5). The first <code>SendError</code> is absorbed silently because the dominant cause is the benign first-message-after-idle race. Only when the <strong>retry also fails</strong> must the failure surface as ❌ on <code>msg.trigger_msg</code> <strong>and</strong> <code>⚠️ {format_user_error}</code> text in the channel <strong>and</strong> <code>Err</code> propagated to the caller. Already-enqueued messages whose <code>submit</code> already returned <code>Ok</code> are residual loss equivalent to a pod restart mid-turn (documented; out of Phase 1 scope to recover). Messages in the consumer's in-flight batch at the time of the panic are also residual loss — their <code>submit</code> already returned <code>Ok</code> before the consumer died, so they cannot be reacted from the <code>SendError</code> path.</p>\n</li>\n<li>\n<p><strong><code>bot_turns</code> runs at ingest, not at dispatch.</strong> Multi-bot loop guards (<code>slack.rs:672-696</code>) execute before <code>submit</code>; batching is downstream and cannot bypass them. Bot-turn-limit counts batches as turns (one ACP invocation = one logical turn); the per-message ingest counter is unchanged.</p>\n</li>\n</ol>\n<h3>6.5 Semantic neutrality — prohibited transformations</h3>\n<p>The following classes of transformation are categorically forbidden because they make semantic judgments the broker is not authorized to make. They are listed explicitly so future &quot;small optimization&quot; PRs can be rejected by reference rather than re-litigated:</p>\n<ul>\n<li><strong>No topic split.</strong> Broker must not split a single arrival event into multiple ACP turns based on content (e.g. detecting &quot;two questions in one message&quot;). One arrival = one event in the dispatched batch.</li>\n<li><strong>No intent merge.</strong> Broker must not coalesce two adjacent same-sender messages into a single event even when they appear to express one logical thought (&quot;see this&quot; + &quot;[image]&quot;). Each arrival keeps its own <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code>.</li>\n<li><strong>No sender collapse.</strong> Broker must not merge multiple distinct <code>sender_id</code>s into a single header even when display names or roles match (e.g. two human users with the same name, or two bots with the same role). Each unique sender event gets its own <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code>.</li>\n<li><strong>No silent drop.</strong> Broker must not omit an arrival event from a batch on the grounds that it appears redundant, off-topic, or empty. The agent decides what to do with it.</li>\n<li><strong>No ordering inversion.</strong> Broker must not reorder events within a batch based on perceived priority, sender role, or content type. Arrival order from the platform adapter is preserved.</li>\n</ul>\n<p>If a future feature genuinely requires one of these transformations, it belongs in the ACP agent (which has the semantic context to make the call), not in the broker. The broker's job ends at faithful structural transport.</p>\n<h3>6.6 Observability</h3>\n<p>Phase 1 emits <strong>one <code>info!</code> line per dispatch</strong> carrying both per-dispatch and per-event values as structured fields — no new dependencies, no JSON formatter change, no <code>metrics</code> crate. Default <code>EnvFilter = openab=info</code> means these appear in production logs without env var changes.</p>\n<table>\n<thead>\n<tr>\n<th>Metric</th>\n<th>Emit point</th>\n<th>Notes</th>\n</tr>\n</thead>\n<tbody>\n<tr>\n<td><code>events_per_dispatch</code></td>\n<td>per dispatch</td>\n<td>Downstream computes 1h-rolling <code>p95_batch_size</code> from this stream</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td><code>packed_block_count</code></td>\n<td>per dispatch</td>\n<td>Total <code>ContentBlock</code> count emitted to ACP</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td><code>agent_dispatch_ms</code></td>\n<td>after <code>dispatch_batch</code> returns</td>\n<td>dispatch → ACP turn completion latency</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td><code>tokens_per_event</code></td>\n<td>per dispatch (as array field)</td>\n<td><code>tokens_per_event=[123,145,98]</code>; downstream reconstructs distribution</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td><code>buffer_wait_ms</code></td>\n<td>per dispatch (as array field)</td>\n<td><code>wait_ms=[42,38,0]</code>; per-sub-message enqueue → dispatch latency</td>\n</tr>\n</tbody>\n</table>\n<pre><code class=\"language-rust\">info_span!(&quot;dispatch&quot;, channel = %channel_id, adapter = &quot;discord&quot;)\n    .in_scope(|| {\n        info!(\n            events_per_dispatch = batch.len(),\n            packed_block_count  = blocks.len(),\n            agent_dispatch_ms   = elapsed.as_millis(),\n            tokens_per_event    = ?per_event_tokens,\n            wait_ms             = ?per_event_wait_ms,\n            &quot;batch dispatched&quot;,\n        );\n    });\n</code></pre>\n<p>Per-event metrics fold into the per-dispatch line as array fields → log line count = dispatch count, independent of batch size.</p>\n<p><strong>Threshold for dedup re-evaluation:</strong> when <code>p95_batch_size (count) × avg_tokens_per_event (tokens) &gt; 500 tokens</code> of per-dispatch <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> envelope overhead on any production channel for a sustained 24h window, the broker team must re-open the dedup question (e.g. emit <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> only when sender or timestamp delta changes). Below that threshold the envelope cost is below noise and the readability win of always-explicit headers wins.</p>\n<p><strong>Phase 1 acceptance test (masami #1):</strong> after Phase 1 lands and is deployed to a test channel, send a 3-message batch and verify the single <code>info!</code> line carries <code>events_per_dispatch = 3</code>, <code>packed_block_count = N</code>, <code>agent_dispatch_ms = N</code>, <code>tokens_per_event = [t1, t2, t3]</code>, <code>wait_ms = [w1, w2, w3]</code>. If any field is missing or events are split across multiple log lines, Phase 1 does not merge.</p>\n<h3>6.7 Batch reaction UX</h3>\n<p>Across all three modes, every message in a dispatched batch gets an <code>emojis.queued</code> (👀) reaction before <code>session_prompt</code> is called. In <code>per-message</code> mode this is always one message per dispatch; in <code>per-thread</code> / <code>per-lane</code> mode the loop covers all N messages in the drained batch. This prevents the &quot;message eaten&quot; perception where the first message in a batch sits silent for 30+ seconds with no feedback.</p>\n<pre><code class=\"language-rust\">// in dispatch_batch(), before session_prompt\nfor msg in &amp;batch {\n    let _ = adapter.add_reaction(&amp;msg.trigger_msg, &amp;reactions_config.emojis.queued).await;\n}\n// StatusReactionController still anchors on batch.last().trigger_msg as before\n</code></pre>\n<p>Applies to all batches including <code>batch.len() == 1</code> — the loop runs once for a single-message batch, making the reaction path uniform and removing the need for a separate <code>set_queued()</code> call in <code>StatusReactionController</code> for the single-message case. The reactions are fire-and-forget (<code>let _ =</code>); failures are silently ignored, same as existing reaction calls throughout the codebase. The 👀 reactions are not removed after dispatch — they serve as permanent &quot;received&quot; markers.</p>\n<p><strong>Sequential, not parallel.</strong> The loop applies reactions one at a time (<code>for ... await</code>), not concurrently via <code>join_all</code>. Both Discord and Slack append reactions in the order the API receives them; parallel <code>join_all</code> would race-order the appends and produce visually inconsistent reaction-list ordering across the batch (M3's reaction may land before M1's in the API's view). The serial latency cost is bounded — each <code>add_reaction</code> is one HTTP round-trip (≤200ms typical), and a full burst-cap-30 batch is ≤6s — small relative to the ACP turn duration this is gating against.</p>\n<h3>6.8 Graceful shutdown</h3>\n<p>On <code>SIGTERM</code>, <code>Dispatcher::shutdown()</code> iterates active threads and logs <code>thread_id=…, channel=…, adapter=…, buffered_lost=N</code> per thread before drop. <code>ThreadHandle</code> carries <code>channel_id: String</code> and <code>adapter_kind: String</code> (set at consumer-spawn time) so the shutdown log can identify which channel lost messages without iterating <code>BufferedMessage</code> contents.</p>\n<pre><code class=\"language-rust\">// in Dispatcher::shutdown()\nlet mut map = self.per_thread.lock().unwrap();\nfor (thread_id, handle) in map.iter_mut() {\n    // drain_pending requires &amp;mut ThreadHandle to close the sender\n    let pending = handle.drain_pending();\n    if !pending.is_empty() {\n        warn!(\n            thread_id     = %thread_id,\n            channel       = %handle.channel_id,\n            adapter       = %handle.adapter_kind,\n            buffered_lost = pending.len(),\n            &quot;shutdown drained pending messages without dispatch&quot;,\n        );\n    }\n}\n</code></pre>\n<p><code>Dispatcher::shutdown()</code> is placed after adapter handles are joined and before <code>pool.shutdown()</code> in the <code>main.rs</code> cleanup sequence. It is synchronous (<code>std::sync::Mutex</code> + synchronous drain) — no <code>await</code>, no timeout required.</p>\n<p>Buffered state is in-memory only; pod restart loses it by design (no on-disk WAL, no Redis-backed buffer). Ops decide per <code>buffered_lost &gt; 0</code> event whether to ask users to re-send.</p>\n<h3>6.9 Scenario D smoke matrix (Phase 1 must-do)</h3>\n<p>Cross-agent smoke verifies that agents correctly read transcript content after the ordering change (transcript moves from before <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> to inside the arrival event, between the <code>&lt;sender_context&gt;</code> delimiter and <code>{prompt}</code>).</p>\n<p><strong>Prerequisites:</strong> <code>stt.enabled = true</code>, <code>GROQ_API_KEY</code> set, Discord mobile to send voice messages (Discord desktop does not support voice message recording), <code>audio/ogg</code> MIME passing <code>media::is_audio_mime()</code>.</p>\n<table>\n<thead>\n<tr>\n<th>Agent</th>\n<th>Test case</th>\n<th>Pass criteria</th>\n</tr>\n</thead>\n<tbody>\n<tr>\n<td>Claude Code</td>\n<td>Voice-only message in a thread → agent responds</td>\n<td>Reply text references / acknowledges transcript content (not just emoji or &quot;got it&quot;)</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Claude Code</td>\n<td>Voice + text in same batch → agent responds</td>\n<td>Reply addresses both the typed text <strong>and</strong> the voice transcript</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Cursor</td>\n<td>Voice-only message in a thread → agent responds</td>\n<td>Same as Claude Code voice-only</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Copilot</td>\n<td>Voice-only message in a thread → agent responds</td>\n<td>Same as Claude Code voice-only</td>\n</tr>\n</tbody>\n</table>\n<p><strong>Decision gate:</strong> if any agent fails to reference transcript content, do not merge Phase 1. Apply the <code>extra_blocks.len() == 1 &amp;&amp; prompt.is_empty()</code> escape hatch (§3.6 rollback), re-run the matrix. If still failing: hold Phase 1, file follow-up.</p>\n<h3>6.10 Per-mode consumer idle timeout</h3>\n<p>Each <code>Dispatcher</code> carries an <code>idle_timeout: Duration</code> chosen per <code>MessageProcessingMode</code> (§4.1). The consumer evicts itself when no message arrives within <code>idle_timeout</code>; eviction drops the <code>ThreadHandle</code> and closes the mpsc, after which the next <code>submit</code> lazily constructs a fresh handle through the same map-insert path used at first arrival.</p>\n<p>Two named constants:</p>\n<pre><code class=\"language-rust\">pub const PER_MESSAGE_CONSUMER_IDLE_TIMEOUT: Duration = Duration::from_secs(10);\npub const DEFAULT_CONSUMER_IDLE_TIMEOUT: Duration = Duration::from_secs(300);\n</code></pre>\n<table>\n<thead>\n<tr>\n<th>Mode</th>\n<th>Idle timeout</th>\n<th>Rationale</th>\n</tr>\n</thead>\n<tbody>\n<tr>\n<td><code>per-message</code></td>\n<td>10s</td>\n<td>The buffer is cap=1, so each consumer drains exactly one message per turn. Once the turn completes there is no batching window to preserve — keeping the consumer alive is pure overhead. A 10s timeout absorbs consecutive rapid-fire messages without the cost of repeatedly re-spawning the consumer task, while still freeing the slot quickly when the user goes idle.</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td><code>per-thread</code> / <code>per-lane</code></td>\n<td>300s</td>\n<td>The buffer fills <em>during the turn</em> (I1) and the consumer needs to be there at turn completion to drain. After the turn, the consumer parks on <code>recv()</code> waiting for follow-up messages from the same thread / lane. Five minutes is long enough to absorb typical user-thinking-then-typing pauses while still bounding the idle resource footprint.</td>\n</tr>\n</tbody>\n</table>\n<p><strong>Why not zero / one-shot for <code>per-message</code>.</strong> A consumer-per-message lifecycle would re-spawn <code>tokio::Task</code> + re-allocate the handle on every arrival, doubling the dispatcher overhead per message. For rapid-fire bursts (the workload §1.1 documents) this is the wrong direction. 10s gives the consumer a chance to handle the burst as a sequence of cap=1 dispatches with one task spawn.</p>\n<p><strong>Why not 300s for <code>per-message</code>.</strong> Per Little's Law (<code>L = λ × W</code>), an N-thread system at λ messages/min/thread × 5min idle window yields ~30× more idle consumer tasks than a 10s window. For batched modes the long window is paying for batching opportunity; for <code>per-message</code> it is paying for nothing.</p>\n<p><strong>Sweep eviction.</strong> <code>Dispatcher::sweep_stale</code> runs on a 60s <code>tokio::time::interval</code> ticker spawned from <code>main.rs</code> alongside the dispatcher; the ticker calls <code>sweep_stale</code> every minute and evicts any consumer whose last activity exceeds its <code>idle_timeout</code>. The 60s cadence is coarser than <code>PER_MESSAGE_CONSUMER_IDLE_TIMEOUT</code> (10s) on purpose: lazy <code>recv</code>-deadline eviction handles the live-traffic case where the consumer is parked and wakes on its own, so sweep only needs to bound the worst-case linger for the corner case where a one-shot consumer never gets a chance to self-evict. With a 60s cadence and a 10s timeout, an idle <code>per-message</code> consumer is evicted within 10–70s; for <code>per-thread</code> / <code>per-lane</code> (300s timeout) it is 300–360s. Each tick takes one synchronous <code>per_thread</code> lock + a HashMap iteration, no per-thread allocation.</p>\n<h3>6.11 SendError manual staging smoke matrix (Phase 1 must-do)</h3>\n<p>Automating an end-to-end SendError test is awkward because the failure path requires a panic inside a live consumer task — which is hard to inject deterministically in CI without making <code>dispatch.rs</code> test-flag-aware. SendError handling (§2.5) therefore validates via a manual staging smoke run; this section is the matrix that run uses.</p>\n<p>Two paths must be exercised: (A) the <strong>happy path</strong> — single panic, transparent retry succeeds, no user-visible signal; (B) the <strong>failing-retry path</strong> — persistent panic where the retry consumer also dies, surfaces ❌ + ⚠️ + <code>Err(ConsumerDead)</code>.</p>\n<p><strong>Prerequisites:</strong> staging deployment with <code>RUST_LOG=openab=debug</code> (so <code>dispatch</code> debug events show up); a thread the operator owns; deploy a build with an env-var-controlled panic injector that supports two modes — <code>PANIC_ONCE</code> (first consumer panics, subsequent consumers run normally) and <code>PANIC_ALWAYS</code> (every consumer panics on first dispatch).</p>\n<p><strong>Path A — transparent retry happy path (<code>PANIC_ONCE=1</code>):</strong></p>\n<table>\n<thead>\n<tr>\n<th>Step</th>\n<th>Action</th>\n<th>Pass criteria</th>\n</tr>\n</thead>\n<tbody>\n<tr>\n<td>1</td>\n<td>Send M1 in a fresh thread; wait for the agent to start a turn (👀 reaction visible).</td>\n<td>Consumer task is running, <code>&lt;thread_key&gt;</code> appears in <code>per_thread</code> map.</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>2</td>\n<td>While the turn is in flight, send M2 and M3.</td>\n<td>Both arrivals get the 👀 reaction; both are in the consumer's mpsc buffer.</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>3</td>\n<td>Trigger the one-shot panic inside the consumer task.</td>\n<td>Consumer task exits; the existing <code>&lt;thread_key&gt;</code> entry is now stale.</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>4</td>\n<td>Send M4 in the same thread.</td>\n<td>M4's <code>submit</code> observes <code>SendError</code> (or a stale <code>is_finished</code> entry — either ordering), evicts, spawns a fresh consumer, and <strong>transparently re-sends</strong>. M4 dispatches normally on the new consumer. <strong>No</strong> ❌ reaction, <strong>no</strong> ⚠️ text. M2 / M3 are residual losses (§2.5).</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>5</td>\n<td>Send M5 in the same thread.</td>\n<td>M5 lands on the same fresh consumer (no panic this time); dispatches normally.</td>\n</tr>\n</tbody>\n</table>\n<p><strong>Path B — failing retry surfaces error (<code>PANIC_ALWAYS=1</code>):</strong></p>\n<table>\n<thead>\n<tr>\n<th>Step</th>\n<th>Action</th>\n<th>Pass criteria</th>\n</tr>\n</thead>\n<tbody>\n<tr>\n<td>6</td>\n<td>Send M6 in a fresh thread.</td>\n<td>First consumer panics on dispatch. <code>submit</code> evicts, spawns a retry consumer; the retry consumer <strong>also panics</strong>; submit emits ❌ on M6's trigger, ⚠️ <code>{format_user_error(&quot;dispatch consumer exited unexpectedly&quot;)}</code> text, and returns <code>Err(DispatchError::ConsumerDead)</code>.</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>7</td>\n<td>Trigger SendError concurrently from two messages while <code>PANIC_ALWAYS=1</code> (script that sends two messages in &lt;50ms).</td>\n<td>Each observer goes through its own retry → fail → ❌ + ⚠️ on its <strong>own</strong> <code>trigger_msg</code> (no cross-attribution). Eviction is race-safe — verify in debug logs that generation guards prevent double-eviction of the same handle.</td>\n</tr>\n</tbody>\n</table>\n<p><strong>Decision gate:</strong> all seven rows must pass on staging before Phase 1 ships. Failures fall into three classes:</p>\n<ul>\n<li><strong>Path A leaks user-visible error</strong> — ❌ or ⚠️ lands when the retry would have succeeded. The retry path is broken; hold Phase 1, fix, re-run.</li>\n<li><strong>Path B silent failure</strong> — retry-consumer panic doesn't surface ❌ + ⚠️. The retry-once bound is broken (looping retries) or the failure path is dropped. Hold Phase 1, fix.</li>\n<li><strong>Step 7 cross-attribution / double-eviction</strong> — generation-guarded eviction is supposed to be race-safe (§2.5). Hold Phase 1, debug <code>per_thread</code> lock + generation field, re-run.</li>\n</ul>\n<hr />\n<h2>Appendix A: Reference Implementation Skeleton</h2>\n<p>The authoritative implementation is <code>src/dispatch.rs</code> in PR #686. This appendix shows the at-a-glance shape only — struct fields and function signatures, no bodies — so the ADR remains readable end-to-end without committing to keep code-level fidelity.
